STRATEGIC REPORT
Chief Executive Officer’s review continued
A simpler, more focused Renishaw
While the benefits of innovation are clear in this
year’s performance, our new structure has also
helped, with three segments that are more closely
linked to our customers and end-user markets.
As well as giving investors a better understanding
of our business, the changes support the continued
delivery of our strategy, with a single leader for
each segment accountable for every stage of
product delivery.
The new structure is having an impact on the
Executive Committee as well, with our new segment
directors, Louise Callanan (ST), Derek Marshall (IM)
and Steve Oakes (PM), bringing renewed focus to
our discussions. At the same time, our two newest
colleagues, Group Human Resources Director,
Clare Nicholls, and Chief Financial Officer,
John Shipsey, have brought fresh external
perspectives, complementing the deep expertise
of other Committee members to help plan the next
phase of our growth and innovation.
We continue to manage our business portfolio
to focus on core products. During the year we
completed the closure of the drug delivery aspect
of our neurological product line and we are
continuing to seek a new owner for the remaining
neurosurgical activities.
Responding to employee feedback
While restructuring the business has brought many
positives, I know this has not been the easiest year
for colleagues. The combination of our cost reduction
programme, followed by the rapid rise in demand for
some of our products, has created extra pressure
on our people and processes. So I am particularly
pleased that so many employees responded to our
latest engagement survey. A 78% participation rate
is good in any year, as was the 85% who responded
positively when asked if they feel proud to work
for Renishaw.
We’re addressing several key points raised in
the survey, including helping people feel better
connected to our strategy, developing clearer
career pathways, and making it easier for them to
do their job so that we can accelerate our growth.
6 Renishaw plc Annual Report 2026
Simplifying our processes to
accelerate growth
We are committed to simplifying and clarifying our
operating model – our blueprint for what we do and
how we work – while retaining what makes us special.
Our new One Renishaw initiative is focused on
developing common processes in our sales, logistics
and finance functions, supported by our new global
ERP solution, Microsoft Dynamics 365. While we
have faced challenges with deploying this system,
our dedicated team has worked incredibly hard and
has done a fantastic job supporting our customers
during the year.
Refreshing our ESG strategy
I’ve spent time this year working with colleagues
to refresh our environmental, social and governance
(ESG) strategy. The purpose of this review was to
refine our goals, remove outdated elements and
streamline our targets while retaining the ambition of
our original strategy. We explain these changes and
provide an update on our progress in our ESG review
on pages 37 to 48. We continued to make progress
against our strategy this year, most notably by
reducing the emissions intensity of the aluminium
and steel we bought in FY2026 by more than 20%
(versus FY2025), against a target of 15%.
Looking ahead
We made excellent progress in FY2026, with growth
in all three segments. We are well positioned in
attractive markets that offer substantial through-cycle
growth opportunities. Our innovation-led strategy to
deliver outperformance is also delivering results, with
significant progress in our emerging product lines.
FY2027 has started strongly as we continue to benefit
from the current upturn in demand for semiconductor
manufacturing equipment. We expect further strong
progress on revenue and profit in the year ahead.

1. Results of Operations and Financial Overview
(1) Quarterly Results of Operations Overview
During the first half of the fiscal year ending March 31, 2027 (April 1, 2026 to
September 30, 2026), the global economy progressed in a manner actualizing the real GDP
growth rate in the 3% range indicated by the International Monetary Fund this month in its
World Economic Outlook Report for this fiscal year, despite facing various challenges. In
addition to trade frictions with no end or resolution in sight and geopolitical divisions and
turmoil, inflationary pressures continued unabated and interest rates rose in response.
Nevertheless, we believe that the global economy has managed to hold up thanks to the
continuing spectacular expansion of AI-related investment, which has induced investment
across various industries, and the unremitting efforts made by companies.
Under these circumstances, we have also maintained close communication with our
customers, continued to provide a reliable supply of products with required quality, and
conducted sales with agility. As a result, the operating income increased by 27%, the
ordinary income increased by 20% in the July-September of the current fiscal year
compared with the same period of the previous year. We will focus even more on business
growth and improved operating performance. To that end, we will accelerate the
development of products that are valuable to our customers and actively continue capital
investments with a medium- to long-term perspective in order to meet the needs and
demands of the customers and markets in a timely manner.

2026/06/01 
TDCC Drafts the "Code of Conduct for ESG Ratings and Data Product Providers" Based on ICMA Standards, Opens for Public Consultation
To address global sustainable financial regulatory trends, strengthen the foundation of trust in Taiwan's sustainable investment market, and enhance information transparency, the Taiwan Depository & Clearing Corporation (TDCC), in accordance with the Financial Supervisory Commission's (FSC) policy blueprint, has drafted the "Code of Conduct for ESG Rating and Data Product Providers." The draft is open for public consultation from June 1 to June 30 of this year (2026). It aims to guide market intermediaries in implementing international standards, gather diverse market opinions, build consensus, and actively promote the seamless integration of Taiwan's sustainable finance ecosystem with international capital markets.

EU Issues New Rules for Funds Using “ESG” or “Sustainability” Names to Address Greenwashing Risk
EU markets regulator the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) announced today the release of its finalized guidelines for the use of ESG and sustainability-related terms in investment fund names, including investment thresholds required for sustainable investment funds, and the establishment of a transition category for investments that are not yet green, but are on a positive trajectory towards achieving environmental sustainability goals.

2023/09/12 
"Code of Conduct for ESG Ratings Providers (Draft)" - Public Consultation
Taiwan Depository & Clearing Corporation (TDCC), since 2019, has cooperated with leading ESG rating providers to establish its ESG IR platform, one of the first dashboard consolidating ESG ratings and accessible to the public. 
Over the past several months, TDCC has referred to the International Organization of Securities Commissions (IOSCO) report "Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) Ratings and Data Products Providers (Final Report)" released in November 2021 and the Financial Services Agency of Japan "The Code of Conduct for ESG Evaluation and Data Providers" released in December 2022, and engaged in extensive discussions with domestic and international stakeholders to draft its own "Code of Conduct for ESG Ratings Providers (Draft)", aiming at enhancing transparency in rating methodologies, safeguarding the rights of users, and promoting the healthy development of the ESG rating industry in Taiwan. The draft is now open for public comments.

The 2021 update focused on, among others, board policies and practices on the selection and nomination processes/criteria for directors, and further guidance for practices with low levels of adoption as reported in the SC’s annual Corporate Governance Monitor reports. The MCCG 2021 also focuses on the role of the board and senior management in addressing sustainability risks and opportunities of the company. Segment Topics
 PVC/Chlor-Alkali Business
To see how the market may develop,
 We keep an eye on resolution of “two Indian issues”: Conclusion of
sunset review of anti-dumping duties on PVC imports and resumption
of imports of caustic soda.
 We look to Asian PVC price rebound, with its strong correlation with oil
price (correlation coefficient: 0.83).
 Silicones Business
 Progress on our capital investment plan (¥110.0bn) for monomers and
polymers announced in September 2018: We invested ¥6.0bn in FY
March 2019 and will be investing ¥47.3bn in FY March 2020.
 Market adjustments have ended and general-purpose market has
stabilized. We will continue to expand our lineup of high-performance,
high-value-added and custom order products.
 Semiconductor Silicon Business
While silicon wafer markets have been going through adjustments, we
see good progress in inventory correction.
We keep an eye on device demand development.
12
Segment Topics (Continued)
 Specialty Chemicals Business
We provide customers with solutions through hybriding our silicone,
POVAL, cellulose, fluoropolymer and other polymer materials
(launching of “cross-material development”)
 Electronics & Functional Materials Business
 Number of motors in next-generation environmental vehicles is
forecast to grow at a CAGR of 24%, driven by increasing number of
vehicles and advancement in vehicle electrification. We expect
demand for rare earth magnets used in cars to continue to grow.
 Market growth is strong for functional materials such as lithography
materials as evident in a recently announced acquisition.
 Processing, Trading & Specialized Services Business
We will create new value through further collaboration with key affiliate,
Shin-Etsu Polymer Co., Ltd.
13
Integration of SDGs and Management
 We will add “contributing to SDGs” as a new guideline to our Group
Management Objectives for FY2019, and we will work on the
following points:
 Providing materials that contribute to solving the problems
indicated in the SDGs
 Saving as much energy and resources as possible to reduce
environmental impact
 We will provide the following functions to help improve people’s
living standards and solve problems in the market:
 Data input, processing, transfer and output
 Network connectivity
 Efficient use of resources and energy
 Productivity enhancement
 Development of infrastructure for a smart society
 Promotion of health

Drive systems for medical technology
Change the world with
a reliable partner
At maxon, we believe that outstanding engineers and technicians
can make a positive impact on the world. This is why we support
them in their efforts to go off the beaten path and provide the
perfect drive system for their ideas.
View the entire range of products online
shop.maxongroup.com
We understand the requirements
for medical technology
maxon drives are used in numerous medical applications. Our motors perform
reliably and with the best possible quality in high-precision devices such as active
implants, insulin pumps, surgical robots, power tools, respirators, ventilators and
prostheses. Drive components for medical technology applications must meet
extremely demanding requirements. Precision, sterilizability, smooth running and
long service life, as well as low heat build-up in DC and EC drives are essential.
maxon’s medical business unit specializes in developing and producing drive
systems for a variety of medical applications. Our engineers are well versed in
the technical requirements of the medical technology industry, whether for active
implants or robot-assisted rehabilitation. In close partnership with our customers,
we develop the perfect drive system based on a modular standard solution or
create a fully customized solution tailored to the customer’s specifications.
Drive components for medical
technology applications must
meet extremely demanding
requirements.
medical.maxongroup.com
Our experts can advise you in the following areas
Active implants
→ Ventricular assist devices
→ Active valves
→ Positioning systems
→ Pump systems
Surgical systems
→ Surgical robots
→ Power tools
→ Dental devices
→ Ventilators
→ Respirators
Pumps and medication
delivery systems
→ Insulin/pain pumps
→ Dialysis pumps
Rehabilitation and prosthetics
→ Hand prostheses
→ Foot prostheses
→ Exoskeletons
→ Therapy systems
Popular products
maxon ECX Speed 4/6/8
ECX-Speed series motors meet the exacting
standards of the medical technology industry
and withstand the constantly moist conditions
and high salt concentrations inside the human
body. With diameters of 4 to 8 millimeters, the
brushless DC motors are particularly suitable for
applications in medical technology, especially
active implants.
maxon EC 9.2 flat
In the medical technology industry, devices
and drives have to be 100 percent reliable.
Pumps and medication delivery systems are
no exception. For example, insulin delivery
needs to be extremely precise, which is why
insulin pumps require a high-precision drive.
The maxon EC 9.2 flat meets this need pre-
cisely. A slightly modified version of this drive
is used in the drive module of an insulin pump.
maxon DCX 10 S
The DCX 10 S is available as a small drive with
preloaded ball bearings or sintered bearings.
The optional spark suppression (CLL) makes
this DC motor with precious metal brushes a
real long-distance runner. The compact DCX
drive systems are used in applications such as
hand and foot prostheses; and they feature high
power density (torque per volume) and are quiet
running.
Power tools – the surgeon’s instruments
The brushless electric motor has two pole pairs, resulting in very
high power density and high torque.

During many surgical procedures in the operating room, the surgeon relies
on battery powered power tools. These tools are used when surgeons need
to saw through bone or drill holes. This is frequently the case in trauma sur-
gery, if hands or feet are involved or in hip joint surgery. With the EC-4pole
series, maxon offers the perfect drive solution for this purpose. The brush-
less electric motor has two pole pairs, resulting in very high power density
and high torque. Another impressive feature is its ability to withstand
1,000 autoclave cycles.

Power tools – the surgeon’s instruments Robots revolutionize surgery
What was unimaginable a few decades ago is now
reality in operating rooms all over the world. Robots
support surgeons during difficult prostate removal
surgery or other operations in the torso. During the
operation, the surgeons sit at a control console, where
they control the four-arm robot. Its instruments are
laparoscopically inserted into the patient through
small openings, where they can be maneuvered with
more flexibility and precision than would be possible
with any human hand. This helps prevent nerve
damage or major bleeding during the operation. In
addition, the small incisions aid in speeding up the
healing process for patients. To accurately transmit
the movements of the surgeon to the robot and have
the robot execute them, several dozen maxon DC
motors are needed. These have no cogging torque
and are therefore ideal for use in surgical robots.

and ready to ship in 11 working days. xdrives.maxongroup.com

Electric drive systems have a major impact on our everyday life and mobility.
More and more people are using e-bikes or electric scooters for commuting
and recreation. Whether on the road, in the logistics center or under water,
maxon’s mecha-tronic systems make things move reliably and efficiently.
Our systems consist of motors, gearheads, sensors, batteries and controllers
and constitute the basic building blocks for complex applications. To meet the
high demands of our customers, all components are matched to each other by
the maxon specialists. In the development of our competitive system solutions
from a single source, the focus is on flexibility, efficiency and quality.

Drive systems for the aerospace industry
Change the world with
a reliable partner
At maxon, we believe that outstanding engineers and technicians
can make a positive impact on the world. This is why we support
them in their efforts to go off the beaten path and provide the
perfect drive system for their ideas.
View the entire range of products online
shop.maxongroup.com
Motors that are out of this world
For more than 20 years, maxon’s drive technology has been driving the Mars
rovers on the Red Planet. Today, hundreds of drive systems can be found in
modern long-haul aircraft. Back here on the ground, maxon and its customers
develop drive solutions consisting of individual components or sophisticated
technical systems for passenger aircraft, helicopters, spacecrafts and even
unmanned aerial vehicles. maxon guarantees the unrivaled quality of its efficient,
reliable and powerful drive systems for the aerospace industry. maxon has been
EN 9100 certified since 2012. This standard was created especially for compa-
nies that develop and produce components for the aerospace industry. In our
in-house laboratories, we test our drives for resistance to vibration, shock, cold,
heat and vacuum.
The name maxon is synonymous with customized precision and stands for an
extensive support network that guarantees the highest Swiss standards all over
the world. Our dedicated aerospace team assists customers with simple appli-
cations as well as complex, multi-year development projects.
maxon engineers have used the knowledge they have gained from numerous
special projects, such as the drives for the Mars missions, to other aerospace
projects and have further developed this expertise for serial production. Our
state-of-the-art technology and extensive laboratory tests make this possible.
We’re opening up entirely new possibilities for manned and unmanned aero-
space technology.
Here on the ground, maxon and its
customers develop drive solutions
consisting of individual components.
aerospace.maxongroup.com
Our experts can advise you in the following areas
Aerospace
→ Aircraft control systems: actuators for small
control surfaces, air and liquid valves of all
types, fly-by-wire control systems, flaps,
air-conditioning systems
→ On-board communication and cabin
equipment: actuators for antennas, window
shade systems, power seat adjustment,
washing rooms, locking devices for overhead
baggage compartments
Space travel
→ Drives for rocket engine valves, solar array drive
and deployment. Actuators for docking and
separating systems
→ Mission-specific mechanisms for research
spacecraft and robotic probes, in particular for
the Moon and Mars
Unmanned aerial vehicles
→ Infrastructure: actuators for docking, servicing,
starting and landing systems, robotic systems
for maintenance work
→ Payload mechanisms: control surface
actuators, electro-optics, gimbal and load
drives, winch and load locking mechanisms
→ Drive systems consisting of an optimized
combination of motor, controller and propeller
for multirotor, fixed-wing and VTOL aircraft
Popular products
maxon DCX
maxon DCX motors and gearheads feature impressive power density, and
their rugged design makes DCX motors a highly dynamic drive for almost any
application. For example, the DCX 22 is the champion among maxon’s brushed
motors. It is easy to configure online and features incredible power and
energy efficiency, which can be crucial for battery-operated
applications. For space missions, the drive is often
reinforced so that it can survive brutal vibra-
tions and impacts.
EC frameless flat range
The frameless motor kits consist of only
a rotor and stator – with no bearings or
motor shaft. With outer diameters of
only 45 to 90 mm, they are extremely
compact. Their flat design, high torque
and plenty of space for cable glands
allow for maximum integration with your
application.
maxon EC-4pole 32 HD
maxon’s heavy duty product range is specially designed for extremely harsh
operating conditions and temperatures up to 200 °C. The maxon EC-4pole 32
HD is ideal for use in environments that are subjected to extreme temperatures,
heavy vibrations or ultra-high vacuum. As a result, these drive systems can be
used in a variety of aerospace applications, such as: gas turbine starters,
the generators of jet engines, regulating combustion engines,
or for exploration robots. The motors are often used in
conjunction with gearheads. For this,
maxon offers the GP 32 HD,
a powerful and robust
planetary gearhead.

Actuators for rovers, satellites and spacecrafts
US and European space agencies are relying on maxon drives for
their upcoming rover missions to Mars.
NASA’s Opportunity rover has been collecting data on Mars for 14 years
and has covered more ground than the length of a marathon race. This
is thanks to 36 maxon DC motors, which were specially optimized for the
red planet. So it comes as no surprise that both the US and European
space agencies are relying on maxon drives for their upcoming rover
missions to Mars. Our products can also be found in satellites, on the ISS
and on space missions exploring alien worlds. The accumulated knowl-
edge from all of these projects benefit our customers here on Earth.

What Australian Strategic Materials Gets Right About Rare Earth Manufacturing
Market Opinion 
Jack Lifton
October 31, 2026 
2 Comments
Last Tuesday, October 27, I visited Australian Strategic Materials’ Korean Metals Plant in Ochang, South Korea. I have been involved in the development, production, and marketing of less common metals for more than sixty years, and during that time I have visited a great many metallurgical plants, laboratories, and industrial research facilities around the world. I have also listened to innumerable presentations by promoters of proposed critical minerals projects. I can therefore say, from considerable experience, that the ASM Korean Metals Plant is one of the most impressive examples I have seen of what can be accomplished when metallurgical engineering, industrial management, and a clearly defined commercial objective are brought together.
The first thing that struck me was the operation’s scale and professionalism. The Korean Metals Plant occupies a complex of approximately 20,000 square meters, or nearly five acres, in the Ochang Foreign Investment Zone, about 115 kilometers south of Seoul. I was informed that the operation now employs 78 people. This is not a speculative project, a collection of laboratory apparatus assembled for visiting investors, or an artist’s conception of a future industrial facility. It is an operating metallurgical complex with installed production equipment, technical personnel, quality-control systems, and the infrastructure necessary to manufacture rare earth metals and alloys for demanding industrial customers.
The plant was opened in May 2022 and has since developed the capability to manufacture neodymium and praseodymium metals and neodymium-iron-boron strip-cast alloys. These are essential metallic feedstocks for manufacturing high-performance sintered rare earth permanent magnets. Producing a separated rare earth oxide is not the same as producing a metal, and producing a metal is not the same as producing a magnet alloy with the chemical composition and physical characteristics required by a commercial magnet manufacturer. Each step requires specialized equipment, metallurgical expertise, process control, and customer qualification. ASM has established an operating capability in the stages of this supply chain that remain particularly underdeveloped outside China.
The plant’s currently reported installed nameplate capacity is approximately 1,300 metric tons annually of neodymium-iron-boron alloy. ASM is carrying out a second expansion phase intended to increase this capacity to 3,600 metric tons annually. During the first half of 2026, the company completed the installation of eight additional molten salt reactors, bringing the total to twelve. A second strip caster, with a planned annual capacity of 2,000 metric tons, is also part of the expansion program. The existing installed capacity and the larger planned capacity must not be confused. The latter depends upon completion, commissioning, and successful operation of the additional equipment.
I was particularly impressed by the quality of the plant’s laboratory facilities. The quality-control and research and development operations appeared thoroughly modern, professionally organized, and appropriate to the requirements of an advanced metallurgical manufacturing business. This is a subject investors frequently pay insufficient attention to. In the rare earth industry, producing a metal or alloy is only the beginning of the manufacturing process. Reproducing the required chemical composition, controlling impurities, establishing consistent product characteristics, and demonstrating those characteristics to a customer is what distinguishes a commercially useful operation from an experimental one.
A modern quality-control laboratory is not an accessory to a rare earth metal plant. It is an essential part of the production process. Customers purchasing materials for high-performance permanent magnets cannot accept uncontrolled variations in composition or product characteristics. The value of a rare earth metal or alloy is therefore determined not simply by the presence of the desired elements but by the manufacturer’s ability to deliver a reproducible product that meets a customer’s specifications. The facilities I saw at Ochang gave me confidence that ASM’s management understands this distinction.
Equally impressive was the company’s commitment to research and development. Rare earth metallization is a specialized field in which incremental improvements in process efficiency, yield, impurity control, and equipment utilization can make the difference between an economically competitive producer and one that survives only through subsidies. The ability to investigate and implement such improvements within an operating manufacturing organization is, in my opinion, a significant competitive advantage.
ASM has also been developing the capability to produce the heavy rare earth metals dysprosium and terbium, which are particularly important in the manufacture of permanent magnets intended to operate at elevated temperatures. The company reported its first commercial sales of these metals in 2025 and has continued development of its heavy rare earth metallization equipment. This is an important undertaking because heavy rare earth metal production outside China remains extremely limited. Establishing a reliable, commercially scalable production process for these materials would substantially increase the strategic importance of the Korean Metals Plant.
I should emphasize that my favorable assessment of the facility is not intended to suggest that all of its installed capacity is already being utilized or that every product under development has reached sustained commercial production. ASM’s published operating reports make clear that production volumes are still being increased and that additional equipment is being commissioned. This is the normal progression of a developing industrial operation. What matters is that the company has established the physical, technical, and organizational foundation from which it can expand production in response to actual customer demand.
Perhaps the most encouraging aspect of my visit was the quality of the management professionals whom I met. I found them to be outstanding. They impressed me as technically knowledgeable, commercially realistic, and thoroughly familiar with the practical problems of operating and expanding a sophisticated metallurgical manufacturing facility. Their approach was that of industrial professionals focused on producing qualified materials efficiently and consistently, rather than promoters primarily concerned with how large their future production might become.
In my experience, competent industrial management is as important as the underlying technology. A metallurgical process does not become a successful business simply because it works in a laboratory. It must be engineered into a reliable production system, operated by trained personnel, supplied with appropriate raw materials, maintained economically, and integrated with customers’ purchasing requirements. The management team I met at Ochang appeared to understand these requirements exceptionally well.
This offers a larger lesson for governments and investors trying to establish rare earth industries outside China. Much of the public discussion still focuses on mineral resources, mining projects, and the separation of rare earth oxides. These activities are necessary, but they are not sufficient. The ultimate industrial objective is the manufacture of useful products, and the essential intermediate stages of metal production and alloy manufacturing cannot simply be assumed into existence.
The Korean Metals Plant demonstrates that these intermediate capabilities can be established outside China. It also demonstrates why their development requires much more than access to a mineral deposit. The equipment, laboratories, operating procedures, technical personnel, management, and relationships with industrial customers must all be developed together.
ASM’s Korean operation is particularly relevant to the proposed reconstruction of the American rare earth permanent magnet supply chain. The United States does not need merely to announce additional rare earth metal and alloy production capacity. It needs to establish the ability to manufacture commercially qualified products, at predictable costs, in quantities justified by actual demand. The experience accumulated at Ochang could help establish comparable operations in the United States.
The question of raw material supply remains, of course. The Korean Metals Plant currently depends upon externally sourced rare earth feedstocks. The development of reliable sources of separated rare earth oxides outside China will therefore remain an important factor in the plant’s long-term competitiveness and supply security. But this should not obscure the achievement the plant represents. ASM has already established a significant portion of the downstream manufacturing capability that so many other companies are still proposing to build.
I left the Korean Metals Plant with a very favorable impression of both the facility and the people operating it. The complex is substantial, the laboratories are impressive, the installed manufacturing equipment is real, and the management professionals are among the most capable I have encountered in this industry.
For investors, the lesson is straightforward. Industrial capability should be judged by what has been built, what has been demonstrated, what can be produced reproducibly, and what customers are prepared to purchase. Announced capacity is not production, and production is not necessarily a qualified commercial product.
Australian Strategic Materials has made a substantial investment in establishing genuine rare earth metallurgical manufacturing capability in South Korea. I believe its Korean Metals Plant deserves recognition as an important achievement in developing a rare earth supply chain outside China.
After sixty-four years in this business, I am not easily impressed by industrial promises. I am, however, impressed by competent people operating real manufacturing facilities. That is what I saw at Ochang.

“Lost in the buyout noise was ASM’s other asset Dubbo that had a LOI from the US….” 
These days we celebrate the 26th anniversary of Dubbo’s first feasibility assessment. At 0.74% TREO (0.88% incl. yttrium) locked in fine-grained eudialyte-group minerals, the rare earths never carried Dubbo. A quarter of a century later the orebody is still the same.
The project has always depended on by-product credit fantasies such as hafnium and especially zirconia, which means competing with hard-rock zirconia against zircon that is easily and cheaply separated from heavy mineral sands. It has always been easy to see for any seasoned rare earth investor that Dubbo won’t fly.
What we are really missing here is the KMP’s track record. ASM’s Korea segment lost A$9.9m on A$0.5m of revenue in H1 FY25. Even after improving, it lost A$2.6m on A$5.9m in H1 FY26. In the December 2025 quarter the plant shipped about 24 t of alloy against 1,300 tpa of capacity. Granted, no plant is profitable in its first three years of operation. For the expansion, management offered a full-capacity number (about US$26m EBITDA at 3,600 tpa) but on direct questioning is unwilling to say at what throughput the plant breaks even.
Energy Fuels raw material strategy is conceptually entirely flawed. Beginning with a heavy China dependence of the Astron Donald project (if in Donald’s monazite price formula payability rises above 30%, it is anyway cheaper to buy monazite in the open market, rather than binding resources and capital in a China-dependent JV) , via the Madagascar project’s China dependency paired with no monazite license and the unlikelihood of ever getting a license to mine Bahia.
All the above is not new at all. It has been carried in The Rare Earth Observer repeatedly over years.

If these newer genomic and AI heavy platforms see broad adoption, they could reinforce the current catalyst of stronger pharma and biotech activity while also diversifying away from slower academic and government demand. Rio Tinto opens $1.4-billion lithium projects in Argentina
October 30, 2026 | By Mary Bailey 
Rio Tinto plc (London, U.K.) announced a major milestone for Argentina’s lithium industry , marking the official opening of Rio Tinto’s Fénix 1B expansion and Sal de Vida operation in Catamarca following a combined investment of around $1.4 billion.
Both projects achieved first production in the second quarter, ahead of plan, and are now ramping up. They will add 25,000 metric tons of annual lithium carbonate equivalent (LCE) capacity once fully ramped up, strengthening Rio Tinto’s standing and Argentina’s position as a leading supplier of lithium for global markets.
The celebrations included a visit to Fénix by Argentine President Javier Milei and Catamarca Governor Raúl Jalil, hosted by Rio Tinto Chief Executive Simon Trott, and an inauguration event recognizing both projects with national and provincial authorities, employees, suppliers and representatives of local and Indigenous communities.
Milei said: “The expansion of the Fénix project is a historic milestone that demonstrates the potential of Argentina’s mining sector. This was made possible by the country once again creating incentives for the production of resources that are essential to the modern world.
“We are proud that a company of this scale once again sees Argentina as a reliable partner and is investing in our country, validating the decisions we have taken over the past few years.”
Trott said: “Today is a proud moment for Rio Tinto and an important milestone for Argentina’s lithium industry, as we grow our position as a leading global supplier. It was a privilege to welcome President Milei, Governor Jalil and national and provincial authorities, and I thank them for joining us to recognize the work behind Fénix 1B and Sal de Vida.
“These two projects build on nearly three decades of lithium production in Catamarca and the expertise of our Argentine workforce. They demonstrate our industry-leading project delivery capability, as we execute with discipline towards our global target of 200,000 metric tons lithium carbonate equivalent annual production capacity by 2028.
“The delivery of these projects reflects the dedication of our people, the capabilities of Argentine suppliers and our partnerships with local communities and governments. Our focus now is on safely ramping up production, delivering reliable, high-quality lithium to our customers, and creating lasting value for our shareholders and Argentina.”
Fénix began operations in 1997 as Argentina’s first commercial lithium operation . The Fénix 1B expansion adds 10,000 metric tons of annual LCE capacity to the existing operation, increasing its total annual LCE capacity target to approximately 40,000 metric tons.
Sal de Vida is a new lithium carbonate operation located approximately 20 kilometers northeast of Fénix, with a target annual LCE capacity of 15,000 metric tons.
The projects form part of Rio Tinto’s growing lithium business in Argentina, which includes operations and projects across Catamarca, Jujuy and Salta, including the Rincon lithium project.
Rio Tinto’s growth in Argentina is strengthening the country’s supplier network. Around 70% of the approximately $4 billion in growth capital to be invested across Rio Tinto’s lithium operations in Argentina is expected to be spent with local suppliers.

Automotive Radar Market
The automotive radar market is being pulled forward by regulation and by a shift to higher-resolution sensors. On June 11, 2026, India's Department of Telecommunications brought into force rules exempting short-range automotive radar operating in the 77-81 GHz band from licensing requirements, letting automakers use the same radar hardware in India that they sell in other markets. On July 7, 2026, the EU's General Safety Regulation extended automatic emergency braking capable of detecting pedestrians and cyclists, along with driver distraction warning, to all newly registered vehicles. In September 2026, Hirain and Arbe announced that one of the world's largest automotive groups selected Hirain's imaging radar, powered by Arbe's ultra-high-resolution chipset, for a Level 3 automated driving passenger vehicle program in China across multiple brands, with series-production radar deliveries scheduled for the fourth quarter of 2027.
Continental, Infineon, NXP, Denso, ZF, Valeo, Magna, Texas Instruments, and FORVIA HELLA are positioned to benefit as radar moves from premium vehicles to mass-market models and as automakers add more radar sensors per vehicle. Opportunities lie in 4D imaging radar, radar chipsets and processors, corner and long-range sensors, and radar software that fuses data with cameras. Cost, validation effort, and system integration are the main barriers, since 4D imaging radar needs more antenna channels and more processing than conventional sensors, so suppliers must balance performance with affordability to win high-volume programs.

According to DataM Intelligence, the global automotive radar market was valued at USD 6.25 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach USD 20.18 billion by 2033, growing at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 25.1% during 2026-2033.
North America holds the largest market share, while Asia-Pacific is the fastest-growing region, driven by vehicle production, rising electric vehicle output, and ADAS adoption in China, Japan, South Korea, and India. Passenger vehicles are the dominant segment, 77 GHz is becoming the industry standard over legacy 24 GHz systems, and the transition to 4D imaging radar is improving object classification, pedestrian detection, and performance in rain, fog, and darkness. Regulations covering automatic emergency braking, forward collision warning, and blind-spot detection, together with Euro NCAP ratings, are making radar a standard rather than a premium feature.
Asia-Pacific: Recent Industry Developments
✅ June 2026: India's Department of Telecommunications issued the Use of Short-Range Automotive Radar System in the 77-81 GHz Band (Exemption from Licensing Requirements) Rules, 2026, effective June 11, following a gazette notification in November 2025. Radar systems in the band can operate without a wireless licence or frequency assignment, on a non-interference, non-protection, and shared basis, with a maximum emission bandwidth of 4 GHz. Equipment approval is still required. Earlier, only the 76-77 GHz band was license-free in India.
✅ September 2026: Hirain and Arbe announced that one of the world's largest automotive groups selected Hirain's imaging radar, powered by Arbe's chipset with 48 transmit and 48 receive channels (2,304 virtual channels), for a Level 3 passenger vehicle program in China across multiple brands. Series-production radar deliveries are scheduled to begin in Q4 2027, ahead of vehicle start of production, and Arbe is also combining its radar with NVIDIA accelerated computing for AI-based perception.
Europe: Recent Industry Developments
✅ July 2026: The EU's General Safety Regulation (Regulation 2019/2144) extended automatic emergency braking that detects pedestrians and cyclists to all newly registered vehicles on July 7, after applying to new vehicle types since 2024. Radar and camera sensors are the main inputs for these systems, and the phase-in runs through 2029.
✅ January 2026: FORVIA HELLA announced at CES 2026 the integration of NXP's latest imaging radar chipset technology into its ForWave7HD high-resolution radar sensors, which use NXP's S32R47 radar processor. HELLA is developing high-resolution, long-range radar with a range of about 400 meters to support SAE Level 2+ and Level 3 automation.
Key Mergers and Acquisitions
✅ FORVIA HELLA and NXP Semiconductors partnered in January 2026 to develop and industrialize the ForWave7HD high-resolution radar sensor using NXP's third-generation imaging radar chipset. This is a technology partnership, not an acquisition, and financial terms were not disclosed.
✅ Hirain and Arbe received an imaging radar program selection from a major automotive group in September 2026 for a Level 3 platform in China. This is a supply program award, not an acquisition, and the OEM was not named.

Continental | Infineon Technologies AG | NXP Semiconductors N.V. | Denso Corporation | Magna International Inc. | Autoliv Inc. | ZF Friedrichshafen AG | Valeo S.A. | Texas Instruments, Inc. | Hella KGaA Hueck & Co.
Strategic Profiles: How Market Leaders Are Positioning for 2026
-NXP Semiconductors N.V.: Supplying radar processors and chipsets for imaging radar, including the S32R47 used in FORVIA HELLA's ForWave7HD, and positioning its RFCMOS radar portfolio as a lower-cost alternative to older silicon.
-FORVIA HELLA (Hella KGaA Hueck & Co.): Building out a full-range radar portfolio with the ForWave7HD high-resolution sensor aimed at Level 2+ and Level 3 programs.
-Infineon Technologies AG: Supplying 77 GHz radar MMICs used in sensors from many tier-one suppliers, including the RASIC CTRX8191F (28 nm) for 4D and HD imaging radar, giving it exposure to radar volume growth across suppliers.
-Continental: Offering radar sensors across short, medium, and long range, with an automotive business that now sits in the separately listed Aumovio, including 4D imaging radar capable of supporting emergency braking functions with a single sensor.

Charlie Aldridge Q&A: From Cannondale’s final chapter to a new beginning with Thömus Maxon
In this exclusive interview, Aldridge explains why Thömus Maxon’s approach to bike development and its team structure made it the right home as he builds towards LA 2028.
Mountain Bike 
Charlie Aldridge 
Mountain Bike World Cup 
Interview 
Thömus Maxon 
Alex Hunt 
30th Oct 2026 
Piper Albrecht, Whoop UCI MTB World Series, Michele Mondini, Giacomo Podetti
For the second year in a row, Charlie Aldridge ended his World Series campaign with a win. Last year it came in Mont-Sainte-Anne; this year in Lake Placid. But this time, the win closed out Cannondale’s era in XC mountain bike racing, like a script written for the big screen.
Aldridge’s season started with promise in South Korea before illness and crashes disrupted his mid-season, building tension as race days began to run dry. Then came the mid-season break and the resolve. After his setbacks, Aldridge won the XCC and XCO European Championship titles before adding XCC and XCO silver medals at the World Championships.
Coming into the final rounds of the XCO World Cup, a win continued to elude him, with a crash in Soldier Hollow ending his challenge at the front of the race. It was all coming down to the final race of the season, and the final race for his team.
After a season full of trials and tribulations, the European champion outsprinted Filippo Colombo on the finishing straight after a fast and tactical race in Lake Placid. It was the perfect payoff: a World Cup win at the end of a turbulent season, and the final chapter in Cannondale’s three-decade presence at the top of XC racing.
While Luca Martin and Cole Punchard have found a new home at Decathlon-Ford Racing, and Jolanda Neff heads to Fenix-Premier Tech , we still don’t know where Ana Santos is heading, but we now know that Aldridge will race for Thömus Maxon on a two-year deal – a move that may come as a surprise to some fans.
Part of that surprise comes from the fact that Aldridge will be the first non-Swiss athlete in the history of the team. But as Aldridge explains, he wasn’t short of options. Thömus’ team structure, its drive to develop and improve its products, and the opportunity to bring former Cannondale Factory Racing team manager Phil Dixon and performance director Kenta Gallagher with him made Thömus Maxon the right place for Aldridge to build towards his long-term objective of Olympic gold.
What it takes to race a MTB World Cup: Behind the scenes at Cannondale
Relentless equipment testing and tuning, detailed course recon and analysis, and a ‘no-blame culture’ are what it takes for this team to succeed on mountain bike racing’s premier circuit.
Escape Collective Alex Hunt 
Ahead of his official move to Thömus Maxon, I caught up with Aldridge while he was back at home in Scotland. In the following Q&A he unpacks the season that was, the lessons he learned along the way, and what comes next.
Reflecting on 2026 
Alex Hunt: Looking back on 2026, how do you feel about the season now that it’s a few weeks in the rear-view mirror? 
Charlie Aldridge: I think 2026 had a happy ending for sure. The second part of the season was really good. The first part was good but challenging in various ways.
In general, I'm really happy with the season; it was successful from my point of view. Second at Worlds , European champion, and a World Cup win is a pretty good season.

SK hynix deepens Japan chip supply ties after factory speculation
By Candice Kim 
Posted : October 30, 2026, 16:45 
Updated : October 30, 2026, 16:45 
SK hynix Chief Production Officer Lee Byung-ki delivers a speech/ Courtesy of SK hynix 
SEOUL, October 30 (AJP) - SK hynix has brought together executives from more than 20 Japanese semiconductor suppliers for its first Partners Day in Japan, strengthening supply chain cooperation following earlier speculation about the South Korean chipmaker's potential manufacturing investments in the country.
The event, held Thursday in Chiba Prefecture, brought together major Japanese materials, equipment and testing companies, including Shin-Etsu, SUMCO, JSR, Tokyo Electron, Disco and Advantest, SK hynix said Friday.
The chipmaker shared its medium- to long-term business strategy and technology development roadmap with its Japanese partners, aiming to help suppliers anticipate future demand and prepare investments and production capacity as the artificial intelligence memory market expands.
The gathering comes roughly two months after reports raised the possibility of SK hynix building a semiconductor manufacturing facility in Japan, drawing attention to the company's investment strategy in the country.
SK Group subsequently disputed reports suggesting Chairman Chey Tae-won was considering a joint semiconductor factory in Japan, clarifying that his remarks concerned broader investment possibilities rather than a specific plant project.
SK hynix has separately said it is examining various options to strengthen its memory business, including additional production bases, but that no decision has been finalized.
Thursday's gathering, however, focused on cooperation with existing suppliers rather than announcing any new manufacturing investment.
SK hynix has held similar events for major domestic suppliers annually, but this marked the first time it organized Partners Day in Japan.
The event was attended by Chief Production Officer Lee Byung-ki, Vice President Kang Yoo-jong, who oversees procurement, and Vice President Choi Woo-jin, who heads packaging and testing operations.
Lee Hyun-cheol, vice president in charge of procurement strategy, presented the company's business outlook and medium- to long-term direction, while Lee Sung-hoon, vice president responsible for research and development processes, outlined key technologies under development and the company's future technology roadmap.
The presentations were intended to give Japanese partners greater visibility into SK hynix's plans, allowing them to prepare equipment investments and manufacturing capabilities in advance.
Lee Byung-ki emphasized the complementary relationship between South Korea and Japan in the semiconductor industry.
"South Korea and Japan have complementary strengths," Lee said, adding that Japanese suppliers play a crucial role in strengthening SK hynix's technological competitiveness.
He said the company would expand cooperation to support the growth of both countries' semiconductor ecosystems.
Kang Yoo-jong also stressed the importance of closer coordination with Japanese materials, components and equipment suppliers as AI memory technology becomes increasingly complex.
"Close cooperation with materials, components and equipment partners is central to semiconductor competitiveness in the AI era," Kang said.
Tokyo Electron Chief Operating Officer Hiroshi Ishida welcomed the opportunity to exchange longer-term technology plans with SK hynix, saying early discussions would help guide the Japanese equipment maker's development and investment decisions.
The initiative comes as SK hynix accelerates production of advanced high-bandwidth memory (HBM) chips to meet growing demand from AI infrastructure operators.
The company reported record third-quarter operating profit of 83.33 trillion won earlier this week, supported by strong AI memory demand and tight supply conditions.
SK hynix is expanding next-generation HBM production and has secured long-term supply agreements covering a substantial portion of its planned output for 2027 and 2028.
As advanced memory manufacturing requires increasingly sophisticated materials, equipment and testing technologies, closer coordination with Japanese suppliers could help the company address production challenges and strengthen supply chain stability.
The latest gathering underscores SK hynix's efforts to deepen industrial cooperation with Japan, even as questions about potential manufacturing investments in the country remain unresolved.

By

Elena Rybakina, the world’s top-ranked tennis player, has officially withdrawn from the Toray Pan Pacific Open in Tokyo due to a neck injury, granting Leylah Fernandez a walkover into the semifinals. Rybakina made the announcement on Friday, stating she is experiencing inflammation and pain that have hindered her performance.
In her statement, Rybakina expressed her regret, saying, “Dear fans, I’m very sorry to announce that I’ve had to withdraw from my next match. Unfortunately, I’ve been experiencing inflammation and pain in my neck, which has been affecting my ability to play at my best. It’s a very difficult decision, as I love playing here and always appreciate the incredible support from the fans. I hope to be back again next year. Thank you all for your understanding and support.”
This development comes shortly after Rybakina secured the prestigious WTA year-end No. 1 singles ranking presented by PIF for the first time in her career. Her achievement follows an exceptional 2026 season, during which she captured two Grand Slam titles.
Fernandez will now face lucky loser Kamilla Rakhimova in the semifinals for a chance to advance to the final. Rakhimova earned her spot by defeating Australian qualifier Maya Joint in a tightly contested match, with scores of 7-5, 5-7, and 6-1. Rakhimova showcased her resilience, coming back from a 5-2 deficit in the first set to claim it 7-5. Although Joint put up a fight by taking the second set, Rakhimova dominated the deciding set, closing it out 6-1 and marking her first semifinal appearance at the WTA 500 level.

Strong third-quarter performance: BorgWarner reported nearly $3.5 billion in sales, a 10.9% adjusted operating margin and 12% adjusted EPS growth despite declining vehicle production. Light-vehicle eProduct sales rose 33% to $630 million. 
2026 outlook improved: The company raised adjusted EPS guidance to $5.20–$5.35 while maintaining its operating-margin and free-cash-flow forecasts. Revenue guidance was narrowed to $14.0–$14.2 billion, partly due to weaker battery-business sales. 
Growth investments gaining momentum: BorgWarner announced nine automotive awards and expects recent wins to support modest growth above the market in 2027. It is also advancing turbine generators, microgrid inverters and battery-energy-storage products for data-center and industrial applications. 
This ETF Weeds Out Small-Cap Underperformers 
BorgWarner (NYSE:BWA) reported third-quarter sales of just under $3.5 billion, with adjusted operating margin expanding 20 basis points year over year to 10.9% and adjusted earnings per share rising 12%. The automotive supplier said its performance reflected cost-control efforts amid declining vehicle production and a sales headwind from its Battery Energy Systems business. 
Light-vehicle eProduct sales increased 33% from a year earlier to $630 million, driven primarily by European demand. President and CEO Joe Fadool said the growth demonstrated that previously awarded electrification business was beginning to contribute to results, particularly as hybrid and electric-vehicle penetration rises in Europe.

"Our adjusted operating margin and adjusted earnings per share performance was strong in the quarter," Fadool said, citing margin expansion and earnings growth despite a declining production environment.

Chief Financial Officer Craig Aaron said foreign exchange provided an $8 million year-over-year sales benefit in the quarter, while the battery business reduced sales by $54 million. The remaining organic sales decline was $58 million, or 1.6%, roughly in line with the decline in BorgWarner's weighted light-vehicle production market.

Free cash flow totaled $195 million in the quarter. BorgWarner used $175 million for share repurchases and paid $35 million in dividends, returning about $210 million to shareholders. The company said it expects to return more than $700 million to shareholders during 2026, including planned fourth-quarter buybacks.

Updated 2026 Outlook

BorgWarner narrowed the high end of its full-year revenue outlook, citing a refined view of industry production, while maintaining its adjusted operating-margin forecast and increasing adjusted EPS guidance. 
The company now expects 2026 sales of $14.0 billion to $14.2 billion, compared with prior guidance of $14.0 billion to $14.3 billion. It expects weighted end markets to decline 1% to 2% for the year, compared with its prior expectation of flat to down 3%. 
The company maintained its full-year adjusted operating margin outlook of 10.7% to 10.9%. Its organic sales outlook calls for a decline of 4% to 2.5%, including an estimated 170-basis-point headwind from lower battery-business sales related to the lack of North American incentives and weaker European demand. 
Adjusted EPS guidance was raised to $5.20 to $5.35 per diluted share from $5.05 to $5.30. Aaron said the increase reflected third-quarter and planned fourth-quarter share repurchases, along with a lower expected full-year effective tax rate. The company maintained projected free cash flow of $900 million to $1.1 billion. 
For the fourth quarter, Aaron said revenue is expected to be about $3.43 billion, down roughly $123 million from the average quarterly sales level in the first nine months, primarily reflecting production conditions. BorgWarner also expects about $10 million of industrial research and development spending in the quarter. 
Automotive Awards and 2027 Expectations 
BorgWarner announced nine business awards during the quarter across its foundational and eProduct portfolios. The awards included engine control modules for a new internal-combustion pickup-truck platform, turbocharger contracts for gasoline vehicles in South America and Europe, aluminum-wire e-motor technology for a Chinese OEM's hybrid applications, three additional e-motor awards in China, and a next-generation high-voltage inverter award for battery-electric vehicles. 
Fadool said the aluminum-wire e-motor technology reduces wire weight by more than 60% and wire cost by more than 80% compared with a conventional copper-wire motor while maintaining peak torque and power. 
Looking toward 2027, Aaron said BorgWarner expects modest growth above the automotive market as recent business awards begin contributing to revenue. The company also expects $300 million of turbine-generator revenue next year. 
The company expects its PowerDrive Systems business to grow about 20% in 2026 after approximately 30% growth in 2025. Aaron said the company's objective for the business unit remains mid-teens year-over-year conversion on sales growth. 
Data Center and Industrial Expansion 
BorgWarner highlighted progress in products designed for data center and industrial applications, including turbine generators, battery energy storage systems and microgrid inverters. 
The company said its partner plans to expand external turbine-generator demonstrations during the fourth quarter because of customer interest. Subsystem UL compliance is largely complete, and system certification is underway. BorgWarner has completed construction of its final assembly plant in North Carolina and expects manufacturing-floor and capital installation in December, followed by production trials by year-end.

He said speed to market is important and that BorgWarner's automotive manufacturing experience could enable it to bring products to market in 18 to 24 months, roughly half the time of some industrial competitors.

It also developed an 800-volt power supply unit for data centers and displayed it at the Data Center World Power Industry event in Dallas. 
BorgWarner expects to be production-ready for its battery energy-storage offerings in 2027. Fadool said customer validation and UL processes are advancing, with engagement across both NMC and LFP cell applications. 
While the company said current political conditions may slow the completion of some data-center program agreements in the near term, Fadool said quoting activity remains high and that BorgWarner sees no long-term change in demand for its products. 
About BorgWarner (NYSE:BWA) 
BorgWarner Inc (NYSE:BWA) is a global automotive technology company that develops and manufactures propulsion and mobility systems for vehicle manufacturers and commercial vehicle customers. The company serves both internal-combustion and electrified vehicle markets, with a portfolio focused on improving vehicle efficiency, performance, emissions, and electrification. 
Its products and technologies include turbochargers, emissions and thermal-management systems, transmission components, friction products, battery systems, battery charging equipment, power electronics, electric motors, and other electric-drive components.

4 min read 
ELEK LTH1! 
Company evaluates a potential northern New York lithium opportunity as domestic supply-chain activity grows 
WEST PALM BEACH, FL / ACCESS Newswire / October 29, 2026 / Federal Actions Put Domestic Lithium in the Spotlight 
Lithium has become an important material in the battery supply chain, including for electric vehicles, grid storage and certain defense-related power systems. As the United States seeks to strengthen domestic critical-mineral capacity, federal agencies have announced funding agreements, awards and project-support initiatives involving companies developing lithium resources and battery materials. Against this backdrop, ELEKTROS Inc. ELEK is evaluating whether a potential hard-rock lithium opportunity in northern New York, near the Canadian border, could fit its longer-term strategy. The location remains under consideration only; ELEKTROS is not announcing an acquisition, verified mineral resource or mine-development decision. 
Publicly Announced Examples of U.S. Government Support 
In September 2023, the U.S. Department of Defense announced a $90 million agreement with Albemarle Corporation under Defense Production Act Title III authorities to support the planned reopening of the Kings Mountain lithium mine in North Carolina and expand domestic lithium production. In August 2024, the Department of Defense announced an $11.8 million award to Lithium Nevada Corporation, a subsidiary of Lithium Americas, to accelerate development of lithium carbonate extraction and processing at Thacker Pass, Nevada. These are examples of federal support for domestic lithium production-not evidence that ELEKTROS has a government agreement or that the companies have been awarded a specific military lithium-supply purchase contract. 
More Recent Project Developments 
In June 2025, the U.S. Department of Energy identified federal awards of $150 million for Albemarle's Kings Mountain lithium-materials processing project and $225 million for TerraVolta's Liberty Owl lithium extraction and refining project. In June 2026, EnergyX announced that it had been selected by the U.S. Army for a conditional long-term lease to develop a lithium-processing facility at Red River Army Depot in Texas. EnergyX described the proposed facility as intended to process lithium into battery-grade materials and nuclear-grade lithium isotopes. The Army-related announcement concerns a conditional lease and planned facility; it should not be described as a completed lithium supply contract or as proof of current commercial deliveries. 
Why These Announcements Matter 
Together, these public announcements demonstrate that federal agencies have used multiple tools-including Defense Production Act awards, Department of Energy project funding and a conditional Army-site lease-to encourage domestic mineral and battery-material capacity. Each arrangement has its own conditions, milestones and risks. Federal support for other companies does not mean ELEKTROS is eligible for funding, has applied for an award, has received government support, or will secure a contract. Any future opportunity for ELEKTROS would depend on its own project merits, legal rights, technical results, permitting, financing and commercial arrangements. 
Evaluating a Potential Northern New York Opportunity 
A domestic hard-rock lithium project could potentially benefit from proximity to North American processing and manufacturing networks. Those benefits have not been established for the location under consideration. Responsible evaluation would require confirming ownership and mineral rights, reviewing geological information, arranging independent sampling where appropriate, assessing environmental and permitting obligations, and testing the practical economics of extraction, transportation, processing and financing. No verified resource, reserve, feasibility study, permit, transaction or production schedule is being announced. 
A Broader Electric-Mobility Strategy 
ELEKTROS is also exploring potential pathways to advance its multi-port electric-vehicle charging patent, U.S. Patent No. 12,522,100 B1. The company's areas of interest span potential lithium opportunities and EV-charging technology, two distinct areas within the broader electric-mobility ecosystem. The patent does not establish commercial adoption, a completed prototype, a licensing agreement, a customer contract or revenue. 
Management Perspective 
"Federal agencies have publicly recognized the importance of building stronger domestic supply chains for lithium and other critical materials," the company said. "ELEKTROS is evaluating potential opportunities with a focus on due diligence, verifiable milestones and commercially realistic economics. We believe it is important to assess opportunities carefully and to communicate clearly about what has-and has not-been achieved." 
About ELEKTROS Inc. 
ELEKTROS Inc. is a publicly traded company on the OTC market under ticker symbol ELEK. Its areas of interest include hard-rock lithium opportunities, EV-charging infrastructure and patented EV-charging technology. The potential northern New York location discussed in this release has not been announced as an acquired asset or a producing mine. This release contains forward-looking statements under applicable securities laws concerning possible property acquisition, lithium mineralization, resources, mining, processing, transportation, government programs, financing, future customers, charging technology and commercial opportunities. These statements are expectations, not guarantees. ELEKTROS has not announced a completed New York acquisition, an independently verified mineral resource or reserve, a feasibility study, a mining permit, an operating mine, a production schedule, a refinery supply agreement, a government award or a commercial charging prototype. The government awards, agreements and project announcements described above relate to other companies and do not imply that ELEKTROS has received, applied for, or will receive government funding or contracts. The rise of the nuclear hexagon and the future of Asian stability 
Look south to the China-India-Pakistan triangle to beyond US nuclear thinking that’s laser-focused on the US-Russia-China triangle 
by 
David Santoro 
October 30, 2026 October 30, 2026

India's Agni III missile is seen during the Republic Day parade in New Delhi January 26, 2008. It has been in service with India's Strategic Forces Command (SFC) since 2011. Photo: Asia Times files / Reuters / B Mathur 
Originally published by Pacific Forum , this article is republished with permission. 
A central problem in US nuclear thinking is that it is fragmented. Washington is laser-focused on the “ three-body problem ”: It considers the US-Russia-China triangle fundamental, and when it does not ignore the China-India-Pakistan triangle, it treats it as a mere “Southern Asia” issue. Washington, plainly, regards these triangles as two distinct, even separate theaters and pays little attention to the second.
Yet these two triangles are interconnected and increasingly merging into a single nuclear hexagon. That hexagon is driving the world’s primary arms-racing and posture recalibrations. Crucially, US treaty allies in Asia – notably Japan and South Korea – are inextricably bound to this geometry, as interactions in the hexagon shape their security and extended deterrence needs.
Other dynamics are at play, but are peripheral concerns relative to the hexagon. North Korea, though dangerous, remains a localized side problem whose posture does not drive significant strategic force-sizing among major powers. The dynamics in Europe involving the NATO and the UK and French nuclear arsenals are important but function as a secondary, alliance-anchored subset of the US-Russia balance. Meanwhile, the Middle East is a prospective, geographically decoupled dynamic where Israel possesses a deterrent and Iran exists only as a downstream threshold state attempting to acquire capabilities.
The US policy apparatus has not adapted to this changed and changing geometry, but it should. Washington’s US-Russia-China myopia should stop. Failing to recognize and address the merging of the US-Russia-China and China-India-Pakistan triangles runs a major risk: that an impulse in the hexagon sparks a multi-directional cascade that endangers Asian and global strategic stability.
The mechanics of cascade 
China is the connective tissue between the two triangles. It serves as the anchor for what might be called “transmission belts”—the capabilities, doctrine shifts, and posture adjustments through which stability or instability in one triangle impacts the other.
A cascade can originate anywhere within the hexagon, however: through major-power competition at the apex, regional frictions involving allied territories or localized subcontinental flare-ups.
For instance, when Beijing expands its capabilities to counter Washington, – or ,conversely, when Moscow deploys novel systems or conducts exercises in Eurasia – it drives the United States and its allies to adjust missile defenses. In response, Beijing deploys more advanced systems, including near its southern and maritime borders.
New Delhi, which perceives Beijing as shifting toward a counterforce capability, fears that its minimum deterrence is at risk. To compensate, India accelerates its development of multiple independently targetable reentry vehicles and transitions its forces toward canisterized, ready-to-launch postures.
Viewing an emerging Indian first-strike or counterforce capability, Pakistan builds its arsenal, expands its reliance on tactical nuclear weapons, and lowers its launch threshold.
Conversely, cascades can just as easily start from “the bottom” or “the middle”: a localized tactical border dispute along the Line of Actual Control or in Kashmir can compel Beijing into precautionary alerts, triggering counter-adjustments by Washington or Moscow.
In this interconnected hexagon, therefore, competitive postures, regional friction points, and subcontinental flashpoints exist in a continuous, multi-directional feedback loop.
The risks inherent in this geometry threaten stability at least in four areas.
Compressed timelines and lowered operational thresholds
Unlike the 30-minute decision window of the Cold War, flight times across Southern Asia are compressed to five-to-10 minutes, leaving little margin for warning, intervention or off-ramps.
When modernization drives velocity in major-power competition, regional doctrines are forced into high-readiness modes—such as New Delhi transitioning its forces from de-mated storage to canisterized, ready-to-launch postures in response to Beijing. Observing this Indian readiness, Islamabad lowers its own nuclear threshold to counter perceived conventional imbalances, turning localized strategic anxieties into hair-trigger operational realities across the subcontinent.
These dynamics are aggravated by the integration of artificial intelligence and automated early-warning systems into compressed decision cycles, introducing acute dangers of algorithmic miscalculation and crisis flash crashes that human operators have little time to intercept.
The support-deterrence paradox and technology trickle-down
Deterrence in the hexagon is no longer a bilateral calculation but a cross-theater reaction trap where capabilities diffuse across regions without necessarily stabilizing.
When the United States fields technologies – such as hypersonic glide vehicles to penetrate Russian and Chinese defenses – those systems trickle down, incentivizing Beijing to deploy similar capabilities, including near its southern borders. India then seeks its own hypersonics or defense systems from Russia. Compounding this, US cooperation with India to balance China fosters a “use-it-or-lose-it” mentality in Pakistan regarding its nuclear weapons.
Horizontal contagion and the transparency vacuum
Multipolar entanglement enables dangerous horizontal contagion: a maritime flashpoint involving the United States and China in the Taiwan Strait or the South China Sea can trigger precautionary military alerts for Indian and Chinese forces along the Line of Actual Control or in Kashmir, creating a continental-scale hair-trigger.
Significantly, because the hexagon is anchored in Asia, any major military disruption in critical maritime chokepoints during such a crisis would quickly shatter global supply chains, semiconductor manufacturing, and commercial shipping.
Compounding this entanglement is a severe transparency vacuum. China’s refusal to engage on arms control creates a black box. Because Beijing does not disclose its arsenal size and modernization trajectory, India cannot freeze its force levels, and Pakistan cannot pause its expansion if India does not, locking the hexagon into an unchecked “race to the unknown.”
The exceptions game, allied hedging, and normative rot
The transmission mechanisms linking these ecosystems are also political and legal. When Washington carves out exceptions for partners – such as the 2005 US-India civil nuclear cooperation agreement, concluded partly to bolster New Delhi against Beijing – competitors respond by establishing their own counter-balancing exemptions, such as Chinese nuclear assistance to Pakistan.
Furthermore, as strategic stability degrades across the hexagon, the credibility of US extended deterrence guarantees in Asia faces stress, driving regional allies such as Tokyo and Seoul toward hedging strategies or nuclear latency.
Combined with rapid civilian nuclear expansion and dual-use technological creep across Asia, these pressures undermine the application of nonproliferation standards, generating a corrosive normative rot that North Korea, Iran and others can exploit.
To manage these risks, the United States should pursue six lines of effort.
Re-linking global-to-regional instability flows
US strategy should account for how major-power actions and developments in the primary nexus interact with regional security pressures. Strategic planning should recognize that while US modernization and missile defense deployments influence Beijing’s calculus, China’s nuclear expansion is driven by its own major-power ambitions and regional competition, just as Russian strategic adjustments and regional allied postures shape the broader security environment. In turn, Beijing’s expanding arsenal serves as a primary accelerant forcing New Delhi to abandon minimum deterrence and shift toward canisterized, ready-to-launch postures.
Managing subcontinental and regional-to-subcontinental feedback loops
Strategy should address the security dilemmas generated by the second triangle. Policy should grapple with how China’s development of advanced capabilities – deployed primarily to deter the United States – creates a security dilemma for India, which in turn drives Pakistan to increase its reliance on tactical nuclear weapons and lower its operational thresholds.
Controlling upward chain reactions and horizontal contagion
Strategic planning should address the danger of upward chain reactions where regional volatility forces major-power intervention. Policy should establish frameworks for escalation control during horizontal contagion, specifically addressing how a localized crisis starting at the Line of Actual Control, in Kashmir, or elsewhere can rise back up to the major-power level, compelling the United States or Russia into strategic signaling.
Overcoming transparency vacuums and information black boxes
US strategy should confront China’s refusal to engage in arms control and its opacity regarding force modernization, which locks the hexagon into an unchecked race to the unknown. As an initial step, and because formal warhead-capping treaties are unviable, policy should pivot toward alternative behavioral constraints – such as pre-launch missile notifications, maritime incident agreements, joint risk-reduction protocols on automated early-warning systems, and regional transparency belts making use of commercial monitoring to manage compressed decision cycles and establish predictability.
Reversing nonproliferation normative rot and the ‘exceptions game’
US policy should address the legal decay eroding international nonproliferation standards while reinforcing the credibility of extended deterrence guarantees to prevent regional allied hedging. Strategy should account for how ad-hoc, bilateral partnership exemptions lead to counter-balancing deals by rivals and generate normative rot that regional threshold countries can exploit. Policy should enforce guardrails around partnership cases, reassure key Asian allies against cascading threats, and champion binding regional restraint norms, including universal compliance with no-test standards.
Institutionalizing cross-departmental policy translation
To ensure strategic coherence, Washington should bridge the institutional gap between conventional military planning and nuclear stability. Policy mechanisms should establish assessment evaluations across key command centers to evaluate the cross-theater impact of proposed conventional arms transfers, missile defense deployments, and long-range strike capabilities before they trigger destabilizing chain reactions.
The main strategic game is no longer restricted to the US-Russia-China triangle. It is now defined by a broader hexagon, with the China-India-Pakistan triangle also shaping the global balance.
Three decades ago, several analysts argued that the nuclear future would be written in Asia. What was then viewed as an emerging strategic trajectory has now become an indisputable reality, even as nuclear dangers exist elsewhere. Addressing this shift requires American policy to build an Asia-centric framework tailored to the cascading risks of the modern nuclear geometry.
David Santoro (david@pacforum.org) is president and CEO of the Pacific Forum. In 2021, Lynne Rienner published his latest book : US-China Nuclear Relations: The Impact of Strategic Triangles .

Karen Andersen, CFA

Smith Collection/Gado via Getty Securities in This Article

Fair Value Estimate

Morningstar Rating

Morningstar Economic Moat Rating 
: Wide
Morningstar Uncertainty Rating
