content_text:
Renishaw completes first phase of £70m Welsh manufacturing site expansion 
Posted on 12 Oct 2026 by James Devonshire 
Share this article: 
Share on Linkedin 
Share on Twitter 
Share on facebook 
Copy Link 
Company: 
Renishaw 
Engineering technologies business Renishaw has completed the first phase of a £70m expansion at its Miskin facility in South Wales, increasing manufacturing capacity to meet rising demand for its precision measurement and additive manufacturing technologies. 
The development, first announced in 2022, forms part of a long-term investment programme that will ultimately double the size of the site, west of Cardiff, establishing it as one of the UK’s largest advanced manufacturing facilities.
The completion of Hall 3 has increased the site’s usable space to 617,000 sq ft (57,350 sqm). Once Hall 4 is completed and operational, the facility will cover 880,000 sq ft (81,765 sqm). The expansion coincides with the 15th anniversary of Renishaw’s acquisition of the 193-acre site from Robert Bosch Ltd in September 2011. From an initial operation employing around 25 people when the facility officially opened in October 2012, the site now employs approximately 950.
Renishaw has invested around £150m at Miskin to date, covering the site acquisition, refurbishment of existing buildings, new construction and the installation of advanced manufacturing equipment.
Meeting demand for advanced manufacturing technologies 
The latest development will help Renishaw increase production of its precision metrology, additive manufacturing and position measurement products, with growing demand for semiconductor manufacturing equipment creating an immediate requirement for additional capacity.
Hall 3 houses manufacturing operations for the company’s metal additive manufacturing (AM) systems and AGILITY co-ordinate measuring machines (CMMs), alongside a multimillion-pound automated storage and retrieval warehousing system.
Hall 4 was initially constructed as a shell building, allowing Renishaw to bring the space into use as customer demand and production requirements evolved. Exceptional demand for the company’s position encoders, driven by the growing adoption of artificial intelligence (AI), means part of the building will now be occupied over the coming months.
The Miskin facility currently operates 134 CNC machine tools, producing around one million parts per month, alongside three printed circuit board (PCB) assembly lines, robotic assembly systems and automated warehousing. Further equipment is on order to support customer requirements.
Our long-term commitment to manufacturing is exemplified by the investment that we have made in Miskin over the past 15 years and I would like to thank the many people from across our business who have supported the development of this world-class facility.
Jim Long, Director of Group Manufacturing at Renishaw 
Sustainability and workforce investment 
The expansion has also been designed to improve the facility’s environmental performance. Both new halls have been designed to achieve Net Zero Carbon in Operation, supporting Renishaw’s commitment to reaching Net Zero greenhouse gas emissions across Scopes 1 and 2 by 2028. The company’s longer-term ambition is for all buildings at Miskin to operate at Net Zero.
Alongside the manufacturing investment, Renishaw has developed an employee wellbeing centre incorporating a restaurant and fitness suite. Improvements to the wider site include landscaped outdoor spaces, picnic areas and a 2km perimeter walking route.
The investment underlines Renishaw’s commitment to South Wales, with additional manufacturing space intended to support future growth in demand for advanced engineering technologies.
“The significant ongoing investment by our Board to increase our production capabilities demonstrates a huge vote of confidence in our manufacturing operations and people, at an exciting time for the business,” Long added.

Exclusive   ​ASML to Raise Lithography Spare Parts Prices
​Samsung, SK Hynix Accept Increase From January; Equipment Price Talks Under Way
JY Han

Reply 0

ASML, the world's largest semiconductor equipment maker, will raise prices by 10% across replacement parts supplied to South Korea.
​The increase covers all parts for extreme ultraviolet (EUV) and deep ultraviolet (DUV) lithography systems. The new prices will take effect for deliveries starting in January 2027.
​ASML headquarters notified Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix of the proposed increase through its South Korean subsidiary in early September, according to industry sources. The increase was finalized after discussions with the purchasing organizations of both companies.
​Prices will rise for everything from consumable parts purchased regularly to major components replaced because of failures or performance degradation. Lithography systems contain numerous components, including optical parts such as lenses and mirrors that direct light, light sources and precision motion-control systems. The increase will raise the cost of keeping the equipment operational.
​ASML has traditionally adjusted prices for individual parts when raw material costs rose sharply or specific materials became difficult to procure, according to industry sources. A blanket 10% increase is unusual.
​"Prices have risen across the board for the components that make up these parts, but ASML also appears to be seeking a larger share of the profits its customers are making," an industry official said.
​ASML separately reports revenue from services, parts and upgrades for equipment already installed at customer sites. This revenue totaled €8.193 billion last year, accounting for 25% of total sales of €32.667 billion. ASML forecast that revenue from this business would grow by more than 30% this year.
​Prices for newly ordered ASML equipment are also likely to increase, following the spare-parts hike. The company is discussing equipment price increases with major customers.
​The Information, a US technology news outlet, reported in July that ASML had notified Chinese semiconductor manufacturers and other customers of a 10% increase in DUV equipment prices, with some customers accepting the change. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSMC), ASML's largest customer, was reportedly opposing the increase.
​Industry observers expect ASML's decision to raise prices across the board, accepted by Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, to strengthen the position of other semiconductor equipment and component suppliers seeking price increases.
​Price hikes are already under way. US-based Applied Materials said during its earnings announcement in August that prices had risen for both new and existing products. Japan's Tokyo Electron also said at an earnings briefing in late July that it was pursuing price adjustments, including for equipment already on the market, to offset rising costs. US plasma power supply maker Advanced Energy Industries likewise said it had raised prices for some product lines.
​The broader price increases reflect a supply-demand imbalance. Investment in artificial intelligence (AI) data centers has prompted memory makers and foundries to expand capacity simultaneously, driving up orders for equipment and components. Suppliers need time to expand their facilities and increase production. Rising inflation and raw material costs have also added to their cost burdens. Unlike in the past, when semiconductor manufacturers used their purchasing power to demand lower prices, suppliers now have greater leverage in negotiations.
​"Large-scale capacity expansion is translating into actual demand, pushing equipment and components into a supply-shortage phase," an industry official said. "As wafer input volumes increase, the materials used in production will also face large-scale supply shortages."

Hexagon to acquire Rocscience for $535m
Posted on October 11, 2026 at 8:34 am by AEC Magazine 
175 
0 
Deal aims to connect geotechnical simulation with live monitoring data across infrastructure and mining projects
Hexagon has signed an agreement to acquire geotechnical analysis software developer Rocscience from TA Associates and the company’s founders and management. The transaction values the Toronto-based business at US$535 million on a cash-free, debt-free basis and is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026, subject to customary conditions.
Rocscience develops software for modelling the behaviour of rock, soil and structures, analysing slope stability and ground movement, and assessing the performance of tunnels, dams and other infrastructure. Its products are used by mining, civil engineering and energy customers in around 125 countries. The software also offers AI-assisted workflows, including a natural-language interface.
The acquisition is intended to bring Rocscience’s simulation capabilities together with Hexagon’s sensor and monitoring technologies, including radar monitoring systems. Hexagon envisages a continuous feedback loop in which live sensor data informs, updates and calibrates engineering models throughout design, construction and operation.

For infrastructure teams, the proposed integration could help connect predictions of ground and structural behaviour with measured site conditions. Hexagon says this would support earlier detection of emerging risks, faster intervention and reduced analysis time. Rocscience will join the Radar & Monitoring Division within Hexagon’s Infrastructure & Geospatial Business Area.
“Its software is complementary to our sensor and monitoring businesses in mining, and increasingly in civil and infrastructure applications,” said Henning Sandfort, president, Infrastructure & Geospatial, Hexagon AB.
“By connecting what our sensors measure with how Rocscience’s models predict, we can help customers move from data capture to informed action with far greater confidence.”
Rocscience is expected to generate revenue approaching US$50 million in 2026, with annual recurring revenue equivalent to more than 80% of revenue. Hexagon expects the acquisition to be accretive to net income from closing and reports EBITAC margins above 40%.

Jenny Hagan,

SIIT president and CEO Riel Bellegarde said the project reflects years of collaboration and a shared commitment to expanding educational opportunities.

A $17-million investment from Boeing is helping expand aviation training opportunities for Indigenous students in Saskatchewan while addressing a growing demand for skilled workers in Canada's aerospace industry.
The Saskatchewan Indian Institute of Technologies (SIIT) and Boeing celebrated the grand opening of the expanded Saskatchewan Aviation Learning Centre (SALC) in Saskatoon on Sept. 25, marking another milestone in a partnership that began more than 15 years ago.
The expansion includes modern classrooms, a specialized avionics laboratory and additional hands-on training spaces designed to prepare students for careers in aircraft maintenance and aerospace technology.
The upgraded facility will also support SIIT's new Aircraft Maintenance Engineer – Category E (AME-E) Avionics program, providing students with opportunities to develop specialized skills in aircraft electrical and electronic systems. 
Expanding opportunities for Indigenous learners
The Saskatchewan Aviation Learning Centre plays a role in preparing Indigenous students for careers in aviation, an industry facing ongoing challenges in recruiting and retaining qualified workers.
The expansion is expected to increase training capacity for future aircraft maintenance engineers while creating additional pathways into Saskatchewan's aerospace sector.
SIIT president and CEO Riel Bellegarde said the project reflects years of collaboration and a shared commitment to expanding educational opportunities.
"More than 15 years ago, Boeing saw the potential in what SIIT was building through the Saskatchewan Aviation Learning Centre, and they have continued to walk alongside us as that vision has grown," Bellegarde said. 
"Today, as we celebrate our 50th anniversary as an institution we can reflect on how far that vision has come and what this expansion will make possible for Indigenous learners in aviation and aerospace."
The grand opening coincides with SIIT's 50th anniversary. Established in 1976 by Saskatchewan First Nations chiefs representing all treaty areas, the institution provides academic, vocational and technical training, along with employment and career development services.
Indigenous students account for more than 95 per cent of SIIT's student population.
Related Stories:
Saskatchewan hosted aerospace and defence forum to boost industry connections 
West-central Saskatchewan positioned to benefit from new trades agreement 
Boeing investment supports workforce development
The expansion is supported by Boeing's $17-million investment through Canada's Industrial and Technological Benefits program. 
The investment is connected to the federal government's selection of Boeing's P-8A Poseidon aircraft for Canada's multi-mission aircraft program.
The Industrial and Technological Benefits program requires companies awarded major defence contracts to undertake business activities and investments that benefit Canada's economy.
Boeing's partnership with SIIT dates back to 2010, when the company first contributed to establishing the Saskatchewan Aviation Learning Centre.
Boeing Canada president Al Meinzinger said the expanded facility will help strengthen the province's aviation workforce.
"We're very proud of what our longstanding partnership with SIIT has achieved, particularly in expanding access to high-quality aerospace education here in Saskatchewan," Meinzinger said. 
"This will help create meaningful opportunities for Indigenous learners and it's exciting to know that students trained at the SALC will bring their talent and skills to the aerospace sector for years to come."
Addressing Canada's aviation workforce needs
The expanded training centre is intended to help address shortages of skilled aviation workers by increasing access to specialized aircraft maintenance education.
Aircraft maintenance engineers are responsible for inspecting, maintaining and repairing aircraft to ensure they meet safety and operational standards.
The new avionics program will provide training focused on aircraft electronic systems, an increasingly important field as aviation technology continues to advance.
Federal Secretary of State for Defence Procurement Stephen Fuhr said the investment demonstrates how defence procurement can support Canadian workforce development. 
"Canada's Industrial and Technological Benefits program is delivering tangible results for Canadians," Fuhr said.
"The new Saskatchewan Aviation Learning Centre will create new training opportunities in the aerospace sector and continue to grow Canada's aviation capabilities."
Provincial government welcomes expansion
Saskatchewan Advanced Education Minister Ken Cheveldayoff said the expanded facility will provide students with opportunities to pursue technical careers without leaving the province for specialized training.
"This expansion is an important investment in Saskatchewan students, communities and industries," Cheveldayoff said.
"Partnerships like this ensure our students have access to high-quality, hands-on training close to home." 
Saskatchewan Immigration and Career Training Minister Eric Schmalz also welcomed Boeing's continued investment, noting the province provides funding for SIIT's aircraft maintenance engineer program.
Schmalz said the partnership represents an important investment in Saskatchewan's skilled trades workforce.
Building on 50 years of education
As SIIT marks five decades of providing educational opportunities, the expanded aviation centre represents another step in the institution's efforts to connect Indigenous learners with employment in specialized industries.
SIIT is a First Nations-governed institution and one of four credit-granting post-secondary institutions in Saskatchewan.
The expanded Saskatchewan Aviation Learning Centre is expected to support future generations of aircraft maintenance professionals while contributing to the province's aviation industry. 
The announcement did not specify how many additional students the expanded facility will accommodate or when the new avionics program will begin accepting students.

Cloudflare Absorbs Entire Deno Development Team, Consolidating Workers for Self-Hosted Operations
Add preferred source 
Cloudflare announced on October 9 that the entire development team behind the JavaScript runtime Deno will join the company. Ryan Dahl, creator of Node.js, and his team will lead the integration of celld—developed by the Deno team—with the open-source workerd runtime, enabling Workers and Durable Objects to run on self-managed infrastructure. The Deno runtime will receive monthly updates for one year before official development ends, while Deno Deploy will shut down after six months. Deno itself will remain open source, and JSR will continue operating on Cloudflare's infrastructure. The move follows pricing tensions that surfaced in August when celld launched with rates significantly undercutting Cloudflare Workers, as well as Anthropic's acquisition of Bun developer Oven late last year.
Key Elements 
Cloudflare Deno Ryan Dahl Kenton Varda Workers Durable Objects celld workerd Deno Deploy JSR Bert Belder Node.js 
U.S. cloud computing giant Cloudflare announced on October 9 that the entire team behind "Deno," the JavaScript and TypeScript runtime, will join the company. The Deno development team, led by Ryan Dahl—the creator of Node.js—will embark on integration work to enable Cloudflare's serverless platform "Workers" to run in full production on self-managed infrastructure.
The announcement was posted on Cloudflare's official blog under the joint bylines of Dahl and the company's Kenton Varda. Deno published the same announcement on its own blog the same day. Neither company disclosed transaction terms, including any acquisition price.
At the core of this integration is making Workers and "Durable Objects"—Cloudflare's stateful distributed processing mechanism—easy to operate outside of Cloudflare's own cloud. In August, the Deno team released "celld," a Workers-compatible distributed execution platform. Going forward, the team will integrate celld with "workerd," the Workers runtime that Cloudflare has open-sourced, evolving it into a formally supported self-hosted solution. Dahl and Bert Belder will lead this effort.
Dahl stated, "I'm joining Cloudflare to make the Workers programming model the mainstream way to build servers." Deno's leadership has decided to concentrate development resources on this shared foundation rather than continuing to operate an independent runtime and hosting service.
Product and Service Transition Timeline
With the integration, a phased wind-down plan has been outlined for Deno's existing products and services.
Product / Service Future Status 
Deno runtime Monthly releases with bug fixes and security updates will continue for one year. Official development will then end. It will remain open source, and community-led development is welcomed 
Deno Deploy Will operate for six months before shutting down. Paid customers will receive migration assistance to Workers 
JSR (package registry) Operations will continue, with infrastructure transferred to Cloudflare 
rusty_v8 Support will continue, with the goal of integration into workerd 
Note: Timeline based on official announcements from both companies.
Deno is a JavaScript and TypeScript runtime that Dahl unveiled in 2018, designed to address architectural shortcomings in Node.js with a more secure and modern approach. Dahl led Node.js's early development before leaving the project in 2012.
celld Fills the Gap in workerd
In the joint post, Cloudflare's Varda directly pushed back against long-standing criticism that Workers creates vendor lock-in. His argument is straightforward: workerd is open source, and the code published is identical to what runs in Cloudflare's production environment. He noted there are actual cases of users migrating away from Workers using it.
"Open-sourcing and providing an escape hatch is actually good business," Varda argued. He then identified the real challenge: workerd's Durable Objects only support a single instance and cannot scale. celld fills this gap, and it will be the core focus of the Deno team's work after joining.
Dahl described Deno's trajectory as a single through-line: "Deno → Deno Deploy → celld." Through operating Deno Deploy, he said, the team came to appreciate just how much complexity lurks behind the developer experience—managing multiple public clouds, multiple databases, and intertwined services. The answer that emerged was celld, a single binary written in Rust.
celld's only external dependency is a single object storage bucket. It bakes all the fundamental elements of distributed processing—compute, relational database, queues, and WebSockets—directly into the programming model. In Dahl's words, "Scalability should be built into the programming model; each application shouldn't have to assemble its own infrastructure."
The reason celld chose Cloudflare Workers' programming model as its foundation is the Durable Objects abstraction. Each Durable Object functions as a small, individually addressable server with an embedded SQLite database, runs single-threaded, and comes standard with synchronous access to a local database and WebSockets. Dahl sees this type of abstraction as particularly useful for agent harnesses—the execution substrate for AI agents—because it combines serverless execution, persistent state, WebSockets, and a high-level JavaScript interface all in one.
Pricing Sparring Two Months Ago and the Shadow of the Bun Acquisition
Deno's decision to come under Cloudflare's umbrella follows a pricing skirmish that surfaced over the past two months. When Deno unveiled celld in August, it offered a pricing structure significantly cheaper than Cloudflare Workers, initiating a price competition. Cloudflare pushed back, creating tension between the two parties.
Additionally, late last year, Oven—the company behind the JavaScript runtime "Bun"—was acquired by AI company Anthropic, a similar development in the same space. The pattern of independent runtime developers being absorbed into larger platform companies continues.
However, there are important differences between the Bun acquisition and Deno's integration. In Bun's case, Anthropic was seen as leveraging the runtime technology itself to strengthen its own AI infrastructure. In Deno's case, the primary focus is expanding the ecosystem of Cloudflare's existing Workers product. It is less an acquisition and more an integration of projects heading in the same direction.
Impact on the Developer Community
This announcement marks a major turning point for developers who have built applications on Deno. With official development of the Deno runtime ending after a one-year grace period, existing users will need to consider migration options. Paid Deno Deploy customers will receive migration assistance to Cloudflare Workers, but no specific support measures for free-tier users have been announced.
On the other hand, Deno's survival as an open-source project is guaranteed, leaving the door open for the community to fork and continue development. JSR will also continue operating, meaning part of the Deno ecosystem will live on atop Cloudflare's infrastructure.
The JavaScript server-side world has seen multiple runtimes compete since Node.js debuted in 2009. Dahl proved with Node.js that "you can write servers in JavaScript," refined that design with Deno, and is now aiming to make the Workers programming model—a distributed execution paradigm with compute, database, queues, and real-time communication built in—the mainstream approach for self-hosted operations. The loss of yet another independent runtime option is a short-term blow for developers, but for the broader JavaScript server ecosystem, it may serve as a catalyst for wider adoption of a programming model that hides the complexity of distributed systems.

content_text:
Samsung's HBM Market Share Jumps to 33%; Hybrid Bonding Technology Could Be Key to Overtaking Rivals
Add preferred source 3 
Samsung Electronics' share of the HBM market surged from 21% in Q1 2026 to 33% in Q2, while SK Hynix retained the top spot with a 50% revenue share, down from 58% in the prior quarter. Separately, an expert interview report indicates Samsung has begun delivering HBM samples using hybrid bonding technology to customers, while SK Hynix is reportedly encountering difficulties in developing the same technology. SK Hynix, however, continues to advance sample deliveries of 12-layer HBM4E using its existing Advanced MR-MUF packaging technology. Hybrid bonding faces significant manufacturing challenges including chemical mechanical polishing, surface contamination, and die warpage — the gap from samples to mass production remains substantial. HBM competition is shifting from simply increasing stack layers toward a systemic contest spanning memory design, bonding processes, thermal management, and advanced packaging.
Key Elements 
Samsung Electronics SK Hynix HBM Hybrid Bonding Advanced MR-MUF Micron Nvidia Applied Materials Besi Counterpoint Research Tokyo Electron DISCO TSMC imec 
In the competitive landscape for high-bandwidth memory (HBM), Samsung Electronics is pressuring long-time leader SK Hynix from two directions simultaneously: rapid market share gains and an early advantage in validating next-generation advanced packaging technology. According to an expert interview published by semiconductor research newsletter Damnang Research on October 6, SK Hynix is encountering difficulties in developing hybrid bonding technology for next-generation HBM, while Samsung Electronics is reportedly already delivering samples using the technology to customers. The interview was conducted on September 19 with a process development engineer from SK Hynix's Future Technology Research Institute; the interview notes state that the content reflects the interviewee's personal views and does not represent the company's position, with the full transcript behind a paywall.
If confirmed, this would mean Samsung is positioned to complete customer validation first in advanced packaging — a critical process that will determine future HBM competitiveness. However, the information did not come from official announcements by either company, and the report did not specify the HBM generation, stack count, or customer details involved. It is therefore premature to assess the actual R&D gap between the two companies, let alone conclude that Samsung has taken a comprehensive lead in next-generation HBM competition.
Notably, SK Hynix's progress on hybrid bonding technology is not equivalent to its next-generation HBM product development timeline. As early as June 18, SK Hynix announced it had delivered 12-layer HBM4E samples to major customers, with 48GB capacity, using its existing Advanced MR-MUF packaging technology. The company said the product achieves a 17% improvement in thermal resistance compared to HBM4. This means that even if hybrid bonding development faces headwinds, SK Hynix is still advancing next-generation HBM products along its existing packaging route.
The real question worth examining: as HBM moves toward higher stack counts, how far can traditional packaging processes meet performance, thermal, and package-height requirements — and what manufacturing hurdles must hybrid bonding clear before it can reach volume production?
Two Technology Routes Diverge
HBM provides high-bandwidth memory for GPUs and AI accelerators by vertically stacking multiple DRAM dies. As AI models continue to grow in scale, HBM must not only increase capacity and bandwidth but also manage power consumption and heat generation within constrained package space.
▲ Basic HBM structure: multiple DRAM dies vertically stacked via through-silicon vias (TSV) and micro bumps, connected to the GPU through a silicon interposer (early-generation schematic shown). Hybrid bonding aims to replace the micro bumps and fill materials at the bonding interface. (Image source: Wikimedia Commons, author ScotXW, CC BY-SA 4.0) 
Currently, traditional HBM stacking typically uses micro bumps to connect upper and lower dies, with fill and protection material processes handling the gaps between dies. SK Hynix's Advanced MR-MUF represents this technology route, improving the reliability and thermal performance of the stacked structure by optimizing micro bump connections and the filling and curing processes for liquid protective materials.
Hybrid bonding, by contrast, seeks to further reduce reliance on micro bumps. The technology directly connects copper interconnect structures on the surfaces of upper and lower dies while simultaneously bonding the surrounding dielectric insulation layers, thereby reducing the space occupied by traditional interconnect structures. Its advantages: smaller interconnect pitch and shorter electrical connection distances, which can improve interconnect density, reduce signal transmission loss, and create conditions for higher-density DRAM stacking. Reducing some intermediate materials at the bonding interface may also improve thermal conduction.
As HBM moves from 12 layers toward 16 layers and beyond, space constraints between dies and thermal pressure will become more pronounced, raising the potential value of hybrid bonding.
Samsung introduced its hybrid copper bonding technology, HCB, on March 17 in a presentation tied to GTC-related activities, positioning it as a technology solution supporting next-generation HBM with 16 or more layers. Samsung said HCB is expected to reduce thermal resistance by more than 20% compared to traditional thermocompression bonding (TCB). This technology direction aligns with the sample progress reported in the interview, but a technology demonstration does not equate to volume production.
It should be noted that Samsung's published thermal resistance improvement cannot be directly ranked against SK Hynix's 17% improvement for HBM4E versus the previous generation: the former compares bonding methods, while the latter compares products across generations — the comparison baselines are fundamentally different.
Looking at the three publicly disclosed developments together, each differs in subject, methodology, and stage:
Announcer & Date Subject & Method Disclosed Progress How to Read the Numbers 
Samsung Electronics, March 17, 2026 (GTC) Hybrid copper bonding technology HCB for next-gen HBM with 16+ layers Introduced bonding technology Thermal resistance reduced 20%+ vs. traditional TCB; a technology showcase, not a volume production or customer qualification announcement 
SK Hynix, June 18, 2026 12-layer, 48GB HBM4E using Advanced MR-MUF Delivered samples to major customers Thermal resistance improved 17% vs. previous-gen HBM4; this product does not use hybrid bonding 
imec & EV Group, May 28, 2026 (ECTC) Wafer-to-wafer (W2W) hybrid bonding test structures 200nm copper pad pitch; post-bond overlay error below 40nm for all dies on 300mm wafers Research institution results on test structures, not HBM volume production performance 
Note: The three disclosures differ in subject, methodology, and stage; the numbers cannot be directly compared across them.
The Gap from Lab to Mass Production
The manufacturing difficulty of hybrid bonding extends far beyond precisely aligning and joining two dies.
According to process explanations from Applied Materials, chemical mechanical polishing (CMP) is one of the critical steps. Manufacturers must precisely control the height relationship between copper pads and the surrounding dielectric layer to achieve nanometer-level flatness on the bonding surface. If the copper surface is recessed too deeply, the upper and lower copper structures may fail to make adequate contact; if the copper protrudes excessively, it may interfere with dielectric bonding and increase the risk of interface defects. Therefore, bonding surface flatness, copper pad height, and consistency across the entire area must all be tightly controlled.
At the same time, particles generated during polishing and die singulation, surface contamination, and changes in surface properties over time after activation can all affect bonding quality. This requires manufacturers to coordinate cleaning, surface treatment, environmental cleanliness, and bonding time windows. In other words, hybrid bonding is not a problem that can be solved by purchasing a single high-precision bonding tool. Polishing, cleaning, inspection, die alignment, and bonding must form a stable process chain to convert successful lab-scale bonding into repeatable volume production results.
HBM's structural characteristics further compound the difficulty. To increase stack counts while controlling package height, DRAM dies must be continuously thinned. But the thinner the die, the more susceptible it is to mechanical stress-induced warpage, which in turn increases the risk of positional misalignment and bonding defects. As stack counts rise, multiple bonding interfaces also mean more potential failure points.
However, there is currently no reliable information indicating which specific process step is causing difficulties for SK Hynix. CMP, surface contamination, and die warpage are manufacturing challenges common to hybrid bonding and cannot be directly assumed to be the cause of the reported development hurdles.
The industrialization of hybrid bonding also depends on the specific die bonding approach. imec has previously demonstrated wafer-to-wafer (W2W) bonding, where two entire wafers are aligned and bonded together. This approach can process large numbers of dies at once, but if defective dies are bonded along with good ones, overall yield may suffer. The alternative is die-to-wafer (D2W) bonding, where known-good dies are first screened and then individually placed onto a target wafer for bonding. Its advantage is the ability to prioritize tested good dies, but picking, positioning, and bonding dies one by one introduces production efficiency challenges.
An analysis by Inha University professor Seunghwan Joo, published on SK Hynix's newsroom, noted that die-to-wafer bonding is moving toward HBM commercialization. This illustrates that the bonding precision demonstrated in wafer-level experiments is not the same problem as the yield and production efficiency required for multi-layer HBM stacking.
Equipment vendors are also refining the process chain around this manufacturing challenge. On October 1, Applied Materials and Besi announced an expansion of their collaboration in advanced packaging. The two companies are combining Applied Materials' process technologies in polishing, cleaning, and metrology with Besi's die placement and bonding technology, with one outcome being the Kinex integrated die-to-wafer hybrid bonding system. This collaboration reflects how hybrid bonding competition is extending from the precision of individual tools to process integration capabilities before and after bonding. However, existing information does not indicate that Samsung or SK Hynix has adopted this system.
Japanese equipment makers also hold a position in this process chain. DRAM dies must undergo grinding and thinning before stacking, placing Japanese equipment maker DISCO's thinning, grinding, and dicing tools at a critical front-end position in HBM manufacturing — by various estimates, the company holds roughly 70-80% global share in dicing equipment and about 60-70% in thinning and grinding equipment. DISCO said that for the die-to-wafer (D2W) process required by hybrid bonding, the company has prepared multiple solutions including plasma dicing, dicing-before-grinding (DBG), and laser dicing; while cleanliness management is more difficult than conventional dicing, it is "not particularly demanding compared to front-end processes." Tokyo Electron has already launched bonding equipment for wafer-to-wafer (W2W) applications and is developing D2W bonding technology, with strong demand for its HBM-related equipment.
In the logic chip space, hybrid bonding has already entered volume production: TSMC's SoIC (System on Integrated Chips) uses copper-to-copper hybrid bonding and has been applied to AMD's 3D V-Cache stacking (Ryzen X3D series processors) since 2022, as confirmed by teardown reports from packaging analysis firm TechInsights. The difference lies in the application context — that involves bonding a single cache die to a compute die, whereas HBM must accommodate more than ten layers of ultra-thin DRAM within a constrained package height while simultaneously meeting yield, capacity, and cost requirements.
For HBM manufacturers, the real challenge is keeping every bonding interface stable, meeting product reliability requirements after multi-layer stacking, and keeping production efficiency and manufacturing costs within acceptable ranges. Successfully bonding samples is only the first step.
Substantive Changes in Market Share
Behind the technology route debate, Samsung's share of the HBM market is undergoing substantive change.
According to Counterpoint Research data, Samsung's HBM revenue share rose from 21% in Q1 2026 to 33% in Q2; SK Hynix retained the top spot with a 50% revenue share, but that was down 8 percentage points from 58% in Q1, with its lead narrowing significantly; Micron ranked third at 18%, down slightly from 21% in Q1. For context, SK Hynix's share was as high as 64% in Q2 2025. Samsung announced in February 2026 that it had begun volume shipments of HBM4 (claiming to be the industry's first) and said its 2026 HBM sales are expected to more than triple versus 2025.
Vendor Q1 2026 Q2 2026 QoQ Change Q2 2025 (Reference) 
SK Hynix 58% 50% -8 ppt 64% 
Samsung Electronics 21% 33% +12 ppt — 
Micron 21% 18% -3 ppt — 
Note: All figures are revenue share basis; QoQ refers to Q2 2026 versus Q1 2026.
Market expectations are that Samsung's share will expand further as HBM4 shipments increase in the second half of the year. According to KB Securities data, HBM4 products are expected to account for 80% of Samsung's HBM sales by 2027, doubling from 40% this year. The market also expects Samsung's HBM product prices to more than double by 2027 versus this year, with its product contract prices the highest among the three major memory makers including SK Hynix and Micron.
From a broader perspective, HBM competition is shifting from simply increasing stack layers toward a systemic contest spanning memory design, bonding processes, thermal management, and advanced packaging. Hybrid bonding holds the potential to further unlock the possibilities of high-density stacking, but what ultimately determines its industrial value is not whether a batch of samples can be successfully produced, but whether technological advantages can be converted into sustained delivery capability through stable yields, reasonable costs, and sufficient capacity.
If the information in this report is accurate — that Samsung has delivered hybrid bonding HBM samples to customers — then its advantage lies primarily in the R&D and customer validation timeline. Entering customer testing earlier helps identify bonding reliability, thermal, and system integration issues sooner, accumulating experience for subsequent product development. But there remains a distance between sample delivery and volume production. Customer qualification progress, mass production yields, manufacturing costs, and available supply scale are the key metrics for judging whether a technological advantage can translate into commercial competitiveness.
At the same time, SK Hynix has advanced HBM4E sample deliveries through Advanced MR-MUF, demonstrating that the traditional packaging route still has a role to play. New hybrid bonding does not mean existing processes will exit the market immediately; the two routes can develop in parallel, with specific choices depending on product performance requirements, manufacturing capabilities, and volume production economics.
In the next phase, what deserves closer attention is at which HBM generation and stack count each company introduces hybrid bonding, and whether substantive differences emerge in customer qualification, volume production timelines, and yield performance.

Asahi Kasei Therapeutics Announces FDA Approval of HOVILPRI® (pritelivir) Tablets for Mucocutaneous HSV Lesions Refractory (With or Without Resistance) to Standard Antiviral Treatment in Immunocompromised Adults
Headquarters of Asahi Kasei Corporation in Tokyo, Japan

HOVILPRI® (pritelivir), a novel oral helicase-primase inhibitor represents the first FDA approved HSV therapy with a novel mechanism of action in nearly 30 years.1-3 
Approval is supported by results from the pivotal Phase 3 PRIOH-1 trial, in which HOVILPRI demonstrated statistically superior complete lesion healing up to day 28. By Day 28, 63% of HOVILPRI-treated participants achieved complete lesion healing compared with 34% of participants receiving Investigator's Choice treatment, corresponding to an adjusted treatment difference of 28.4% (95% CI: 9.6, 47.3; p=0.0047).1,4 
As an oral therapy, HOVILPRI provides a non-intravenous treatment option for eligible immunocompromised adult patients with refractory (with or without resistance) HSV infection.1 
Pritelivir was granted Fast Track designation by the FDA along with Breakthrough Therapy designation and the New Drug Application received Priority Review.5,6 
TOKYO, October 09, 2026 --( BUSINESS WIRE )--Asahi Kasei Therapeutics, Inc., the global specialty pharmaceutical business of Tokyo-based Asahi Kasei, with U.S. and European business headquarters in Cary, North Carolina, today announced that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved HOVILPRI® (pritelivir) 100 mg tablets for the treatment of mucocutaneous lesions caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection that is refractory (with or without documented resistance) to treatment with acyclovir, valacyclovir, or famciclovir in immunocompromised adults. HOVILPRI, a novel helicase-primase inhibitor, was developed by AiCuris Anti-infective Cures AG, which is now a part of Asahi Kasei Therapeutics.1,2 
"Today's approval delivers the first FDA-approved treatment for refractory mucocutaneous HSV lesions with a novel mechanism of action in nearly 30 years and marks an important advancement for immunocompromised adults," said Stacy Wheeler, Chief Executive Officer of Asahi Kasei Therapeutics in the U.S. and Europe. "HOVILPRI offers a new oral treatment option for adult patients with a persistent, difficult-to-treat disease."1,3,7-10 
In immunocompetent adults, HSV infection is often asymptomatic or associated with mild disease. In immunocompromised adults, including hematopoietic stem cell and solid organ transplant recipients, people living with HIV, and patients with malignancies or autoimmune and inflammatory conditions, HSV infection can occur more frequently and may be more severe. Refractory HSV infection can result in prolonged and difficult-to-treat mucocutaneous disease.7-10 Because nucleoside analogue therapies such as acyclovir require activation by the viral thymidine kinase (TK) enzyme, mutations in TK can reduce susceptibility to these treatments in some patients.2,9 When HSV infection does not improve with nucleoside analogue therapy, available treatment options have often required intravenous administration and may present additional treatment-management challenges for patients and healthcare teams.8-10 HOVILPRI is a helicase-primase inhibitor with a mechanism of action distinct from nucleoside analogue therapies.1,2 
Story Continues 
The approval is supported by results from PRIOH-1 Part C, the pivotal Phase 3 randomized, open-label, comparator-controlled superiority trial in immunocompromised adults with mucocutaneous HSV infection that was refractory, with or without documented resistance, to acyclovir, valacyclovir, or famciclovir. The trial met its primary efficacy endpoint, demonstrating superiority of HOVILPRI over Investigator's Choice treatment, after up to 28 days of treatment. By Day 28, HOVILPRI achieved a significantly higher rate of complete lesion healing vs Investigator's Choice (63% vs 34% respectively, corresponding to an adjusted treatment difference of 28.4% (95% CI: 9.6, 47.3; p=0.0047). Up to day 42, the observed response rates were 82% for HOVILPRI and 42% for Investigator's Choice treatment, corresponding to an adjusted treatment difference of 40.0% (95% CI: 22.7, 57.7).1,4 
In Part C of the pivotal Phase 3 PRIOH-1 trial, adverse reactions were reported less frequently in participants treated with HOVILPRI compared with Investigator's Choice treatment (22% vs. 54%). Discontinuations due to adverse drug reactions were also less frequent with HOVILPRI compared with Investigator's Choice treatment (2% vs. 20%). The most common adverse reaction was headache, occurring in 6% of patients taking HOVILPRI and 4% of patients taking Investigators Choice.1 
"In patients with blood cancers or those who have undergone stem cell transplantation, refractory HSV infections can be prolonged, painful, and difficult to treat, while available intravenous treatments carry substantial risks," said Genovefa Papanicolaou, MD, Clinical Director of Infectious Disease Service at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center and Professor at Weill Cornell College of Medicine, and a PRIOH-1 investigator. "In PRIOH-1, pritelivir demonstrated superior lesion healing compared with Investigator's Choice treatment up to day 28."1,4,7-10 
"Refractory HSV can be a serious clinical challenge for immunocompromised adults, a population with limited treatment options," said Carl Kraus, Chief Medical Officer at Asahi Kasei Therapeutics. "The approval of HOVILPRI reflects years of clinical research in refractory HSV and reinforces our commitment to advancing scientifically differentiated medicines for patients whose conditions remain difficult to treat. We are grateful to the patients, investigators, clinical teams, and scientific community whose contributions made this milestone possible."1,4,7-10 
HOVILPRI is expected to be available in the United States before the end of 2026. U.S. Healthcare providers can learn more about HOVILPRI at www.hovilprihcp.com . 
About the PRIOH-1 Trial 
PRIOH-1 (NCT03073967 / Eudra-CT 2023-510088-37-00) is a global, controlled, open-label, comparative trial evaluating pritelivir in immunocompromised adults with refractory or resistant HSV infection. The registrational Phase 3 portion (Part C) randomized and treated 101 immunocompromised adults with mucocutaneous HSV infection that was refractory with or without documented resistance to acyclovir, valacyclovir, or famciclovir. This included hematopoietic cell and solid organ transplant recipients, patients with malignancies, autoimmune or inflammatory disorders, and people living with HIV. Participants received either oral pritelivir (400 mg loading dose on Day 1 followed by 100 mg once daily) or Investigator's Choice treatment (IV foscarnet, IV/topical cidofovir, or 5% topical imiquimod) for up to 28 days, with treatment extended to 42 days if lesions were improving. Pritelivir met its primary endpoint demonstrating statistically significant superiority in lesion healing up to Day 28 compared with Investigator's Choice treatment.1,4 
About Herpes Simplex Virus 
Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) includes two types, HSV-1 and HSV-2, both of which cause lifelong infections; there is no cure. HSV-1 most commonly causes labial herpes, while HSV-2 is the primary cause of genital herpes. Although many people with HSV infection never develop symptoms, the virus can reactivate to cause recurrent, painful lesions and may cause complications in certain cases.11-12 HSV represents a substantial global public health burden: an estimated 3.8 billion people under the age of 50 (64% of the global population) were infected with HSV-1 in 2020, and approximately 520 million people aged 15 to 49 were living with HSV-2.11 The disease burden is particularly high in immunocompromised patients, whose weakened immune systems leave them at increased risk of more frequent, more severe, and treatment-refractory HSV infections.7,9-10 
About HOVILPRI (pritelivir) 
HOVILPRI is an orally administered HSV helicase-primase inhibitor indicated for the treatment of mucocutaneous lesions caused by HSV infection that is refractory, with or without documented resistance, to acyclovir, valacyclovir, or famciclovir in immunocompromised adults. HOVILPRI is active against both HSV-1 and HSV-2, including strains resistant to nucleoside analogs and foscarnet. In the pivotal Phase 3 PRIOH-1 trial, HOVILPRI demonstrated statistically significant superiority in lesion healing up to day 28 compared to Investigator's Choice treatment. The most common adverse reaction reported with HOVILPRI was headache.1-2,4 
INDICATION AND IMPORTANT SAFETY INFORMATION FOR US AUDIENCE 
Indication 
HOVILPRI (pritelivir) tablets is indicated in immunocompromised adults for the treatment of mucocutaneous lesions caused by herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection that is refractory (with or without documented resistance) to treatment with acyclovir, valacyclovir, or famciclovir. 
Important Safety Information 
Warnings and Precautions 
Drug Interactions With Acid-reducing Agents: Concomitant use of HOVILPRI with certain acid-reducing agents may reduce pritelivir exposure, potentially resulting in reduced therapeutic effect and development of resistance. Avoid concomitant use with certain proton pump inhibitors, and stagger concomitant use with H2-receptor antagonists and antacids. 
Adverse Reactions: In clinical studies, the adverse reaction (all grades) occurring in more than 5% of participants receiving HOVILPRI was headache, which occurred in 6% and 4% of the HOVILPRI and Investigator's Choice participants, respectively. 
Drug Interactions: 
Pritelivir is a breast cancer resistance protein (BCRP) inhibitor. Co-administration of HOVILPRI with a BCRP substrate may increase the plasma concentrations of the BCRP substrate, which may increase the risk of adverse reactions. 
Concomitant use of acid-reducing agents may elevate gastric pH and decrease the systemic bioavailability of HOVILPRI, which may reduce its effectiveness or cause drug resistance to HOVILPRI. Avoid concomitant use with esomeprazole or rabeprazole. Avoid concomitant use with omeprazole or lansoprazole at daily doses above 20 mg, or with pantoprazole at daily doses above 40 mg. Take HOVILPRI at least 2 hours before or 12 hours after H2-receptor antagonists. Take HOVILPRI at least 2 hours before or 2 hours after antacids. 
Please see full Prescribing Information at https://www.hovilprihcp.com/pdf/prescribing-information.pdf . 
About Asahi Kasei Therapeutics 
Asahi Kasei Therapeutics is the global specialty pharmaceutical business of Tokyo-based Asahi Kasei. We are identifying, developing and commercializing innovative medicines for diseases with significant unmet medical needs. Drawing upon our strong heritage of scientific innovation, we are expanding therapeutic options and helping to positively impact health in immunology, nephrology, transplantation, and infectious diseases. For more information, visit: https://www.aktx.com. 
About Asahi Kasei 
Asahi Kasei is a diversified global company that contributes to life and living for people around the world. Since its foundation in 1922, with businesses in ammonia and cellulose fiber, Asahi Kasei has consistently grown through proactive portfolio transformation to meet the evolving needs of every age. With 50,000 employees worldwide, the company contributes to sustainability by providing solutions to the world's challenges across its three business sectors: Healthcare, Homes, and Material. For more information, visit https://www.asahi-kasei.com/ . 
Asahi Kasei positions Pharmaceuticals as a First Priority business in its medium-term management plan, emphasizing value creation by expanding its research and development activities globally to deliver innovative therapeutic options worldwide.

HyProMag USA Notes EU Strategic Project Designation for HyProMag GMBH
HyProMag USA
European Commission recognition supports the development of rare earth magnet recycling capacity in Europe and complements HyProMag USA’s efforts to establish a domestic U.S. supply chain for recycled rare earth magnetic materials 
DALLAS-FORT WORTH, TX / ACCESS Newswire / October 9, 2026 / HyProMag USA LLC (“HyProMag USA” or the “Company”) is pleased to note the selection of HyProMag GmbH as a Strategic Project under the European Union’s Critical Raw Materials Act (“CRMA”). HyProMag GmbH was included among 46 Strategic Projects announced by the European Commission to support the development of critical raw materials supply chains across Europe. i 
The European Commission stated that the selected projects are intended to contribute to the European Union’s objectives of strengthening critical raw materials value chains, increasing processing and recycling capacity, enhancing competitiveness and improving supply chain resilience.
Julian Treger, Chief Executive Officer of CoTec Holdings Corp., commented: “ The designation of HyProMag GmbH as a Strategic Project reflects the growing recognition of rare earth magnet recycling as an important component of critical minerals supply chains. The development of recycling capacity in Europe is complementary to HyProMag USA’s objective of establishing a domestic source of recycled rare earth magnetic materials in the United States.” 
About HyProMag USA 
HyProMag USA is developing advanced rare earth magnet recycling and manufacturing operations to establish a secure domestic U.S. supply chain for NdFeB magnets, essential components for AI infrastructure, defense systems, robotics, electric vehicles, and advanced electronics. Leveraging the revolutionary HPMS technology, developed over 15 years with over US$100 million in R&D investment, the company delivers faster magnet-to-magnet short-loop recycling that uses 88% less energy and reduces carbon emissions by 85% compared to conventional methods. HPMS accepts a wide range of magnet-bearing feedstocks – including end-of-life EV motors, data-center and industrial equipment, consumer electronics, and manufacturing scrap – enabling recovery of magnet-grade material without chemical processing.
Ownership 
HyProMag USA LLC is owned 50:50 by CoTec Holdings Corp. (TSXV:CTH)(OTCQX:CTHCF) (“CoTec”) and HyProMag Limited. HyProMag Limited is 100% owned by Maginito Limited which is owned on a 79.4%/20.6% basis by Mkango Magnetic Materials Limited (AIM:MKA)(TSXV:MKA) and CoTec.

Market Dynamics 
Rising adoption of cell-based research technologies across pharmaceutical and biotechnology applications is contributing to the expansion of the cell culture instruments industry. Growing adoption of automated cell culture systems and bioreactors is enabling greater process control, reproducibility, scalability, and efficiency in research and biomanufacturing. In addition, expanding use of three-dimensional cell cultures, organoids, and other human-relevant models for drug screening, toxicity assessment, and disease research is supporting market growth.
Driver: Increasing Adoption of Automated Cell Culture Systems 
The industry is being driven by improvements in the efficiency, consistency, and scalability of cell cultivation and expansion workflows. Automated systems can continuously monitor culture conditions and adjust parameters such as nutrient supply, pH, dissolved oxygen, and other critical variables, reducing manual intervention and supporting reproducible cell growth. For instance, in March 2026, PHCbi launched the LiCellGrow Cell Expansion System for research use in Japan and other select countries worldwide. The system uses in-line monitoring to continuously measure glucose and lactate concentrations and automatically control culture conditions, supporting efficient and reproducible cell expansion for cell and gene therapy development. The launch demonstrates the increasing integration of real-time monitoring and automated process control into cell culture instruments, particularly for advanced cell therapy applications.
“We are excited to launch LiCellGrow and offer therapy developers a new way to solve common challenges in quality, cost, and delivery of cell and gene therapies. Building on the success of our research-use system LiCellMo, LiCellGrow represents an important step forward in making CGT manufacturing efficient, reliable, and scalable. We are committed to expanding our PHCbi offerings to continue to contribute to the adoption of CGT and other advanced therapy options for hard-to-treat conditions.” 
- Chikara Takauo, Director of PHC Corporation and Head of the Biomedical Division. 
In addition, the increasing adoption of automated cell culture systems is driven by their ability to improve workflow efficiency, process consistency, scalability, and real-time control while reducing reliance on manual intervention. These capabilities are particularly relevant to advanced cell and gene therapy workflows, where reproducibility, process monitoring, and efficient scale-up are critical. The key operational and end-user benefits associated with automated cell culture systems are summarized below.

Restraint: Risk of Contamination and Inconsistent Culture Conditions 
Contamination and inconsistent culture conditions may constrain the cell culture instruments industry by increasing culture losses, necessitating repeated experiments, and increasing laboratory operating requirements. According to an article published by Thermo Fisher Scientific in November 2025, contamination and inconsistent results can lead to discarded cells and repeated experiments, increasing research costs and time. The article also highlights that variations in temperature, CO₂ concentration, and humidity can affect cell growth and reproducibility, particularly for sensitive primary and stem cell cultures. Maintaining stable culture conditions, therefore, requires regular monitoring, equipment maintenance, and effective contamination-control measures, which can increase the operational burden associated with cell culture instruments.
Opportunity: Expansion of Advanced Cell Culture Platforms for Precision Medicine and Drug Discovery 
The expansion of advanced cell culture platforms for precision medicine and drug discovery is creating opportunities in the global market by increasing demand for systems that support physiologically relevant, controlled cell culture models. The growing use of organoids and spheroids in drug discovery, disease modeling, and personalized medicine is supporting demand for specialized platforms for continuous culture, nutrient delivery, and environmental control. For instance, in September 2025, Advanced Biomed launched the A+PerfusC Integrated Perfusion 3D Cell Culture Platform, which combines automated perfusion with environmental control and is designed to support continuous, hands-free culture of spheroids and organoids for precision medicine and drug discovery. The expansion of these advanced 3D culture applications is expected to support demand for specialized cell culture instruments across research and drug development.
“Traditional static cell culture often leads to uneven nutrient delivery and waste buildup, compromising cell growth, viability, and reproducibility. Notably, in certain high-density culture scenarios, particularly within multi-microwell 3D culture devices, metabolic waste can rapidly accumulate inside the micro-grooves, requiring more frequent medium replacement, which can be labor-intensive to preserve culture quality. Our 3D culture system evenly delivers nutrients and clears waste, reducing cellular stress, boosting long-term viability, and more accurately mimicking the complexity of human tissue for improved drug response and disease modeling. The Company plans to scale up the A+PerfusC system for high-throughput use and integrate imaging with AI-driven analytics, aiming to accelerate tumor profiling, refine cell therapy protocols, and advance personalized treatment development.” 
- Dr. Yi Lu, CEO, Advanced Biomed Inc. 
 
Market Concentration & Characteristics 
The degree of innovation in the global market is high, driven by advances in live-cell imaging , 3D cell culture analysis, confocal microscopy, and high-throughput monitoring technologies. For instance, in July 2025, Sartorius launched the Incucyte CX3 Live-Cell Analysis System, featuring confocal fluorescence imaging for continuous analysis of complex 3D cell cultures and real-time analysis of up to six microplates in parallel. The system enables non-invasive monitoring of cell growth, morphology, and phenotypic changes while maintaining cultures in a controlled environment, enhancing the efficiency and quality of 3D cell culture research.
“3D cell research is rapidly growing, yet scientists still lack the necessary tools or expertise to develop, validate, and perform 3D cell assays at scale. We developed the Incucyte CX3 system and paired it with easy-to-use software to make studying 3D models more accessible than ever. Now, every scientist can gain a deeper understanding of cell health, growth, and morphology, while benefiting from throughput that is unmatched in the market.” 
Lindy O’Clair, Product Manager of Incucyte Systems at Sartorius.

For instance, in December 2024, Demcon acquired a majority stake in Orgonex, a Utrecht University spin-off that developed a compact bioreactor specifically for organoid cultivation. The acquisition strengthened Demcon’s cell culture technology portfolio and provided resources for further product development and commercialization. Moreover, Orgonex’s bioreactor is designed to improve cultivation efficiency and can be integrated into existing laboratory infrastructure, supporting its adoption in academic, biotechnology, and pharmaceutical research.

The market is witnessing product expansion with the introduction of advanced bioreactor systems that enhance flexibility, automation, and process monitoring. For instance, in March 2025, Culture Biosciences launched the Stratyx 250, a mobile, cloud-integrated bioreactor specifically designed for cell culture process development. The system combines automated control, remote monitoring, and cloud-based data visibility, expanding access to the flexible, digitally connected bioreactor solutions for cell culture research and process development.
“The biotech and biopharmaceutical market segments are experiencing a major shift toward cloud-powered, modular bioprocessing, and these companies need hardware and software that can keep up. With a five-month ROI timeline and a plug-and-play scalable architecture, our platform offers a cost-effective, flexible alternative to traditional bioreactors, helping companies accelerate development and reduce costs without compromising on quality.” 
- Chris Williams, CEO of Culture Biosciences

Companies are expanding into emerging markets to address growing demand for cell culture systems, incubators, bioreactors, cell expansion systems, cell analysis instruments, and cell processing equipment, improving product availability and supporting growth in life sciences research and biopharmaceutical development.

The cell culture instruments market is expected to experience moderate growth, driven by the increasing need for efficient, standardized, and scalable cell culture workflows across research and bioprocessing applications. As end users seek greater operational efficiency, demand is expected to shift toward instruments that deliver consistent performance, enable flexible workflow integration, and reduce manual intervention. The market is also likely to benefit from growing emphasis on simplifying complex cell culture processes and improving the utilization of laboratory resources. Manufacturers are focusing on developing modular, application-oriented solutions that accommodate changing throughput requirements while enabling seamless integration across cell culture workflows.

The system integrates robotic cell processing with approximately 100 independent incubation units and automates processes including media exchange, cell seeding, and passaging. Moreover, the system supports commercial-scale cell manufacturing with a processing capacity of up to 24 batches per day, highlighting the growing adoption of automated cell culture systems.
The cell processing instruments segment is expected to grow at the fastest CAGR during the forecast period, driven by the increasing adoption of automated cell-processing technologies. For instance, in January 2025, Curiox Biosystems launched the C-Free Pluto ALPHA, an automated cell washing system designed to replace conventional centrifuge-based washing of suspension cells and beads. The system uses a pipette head to provide consistent cell washing while reducing manual handling. -Dr. Namyong Kim, CEO & CTO at Curiox Biosystems

The biopharmaceutical production segment led the market with the largest revenue share of 44.6% in 2025. Arkema invests €10 million in its global battery R&D center of excellence in the Lyon region
09-Oct-2026 
Advertisement

The Standard for Lab Zeta Potential Measurement 
Your entry into laboratory automation 
Arkema continues to invest in the battery business value chain and announces a €10 million expansion project for its Global Battery Center of Excellence located in Oullins-Pierre-Bénite, in the Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes region of France.
Arkema
This investment reflects the Group’s strategy of continuously strengthening its research capabilities in advanced materials for batteries within its global network of R &D laboratories covering the entire battery value chain.
Following the inauguration in Normandy in September 2025 of a laboratory dedicated to solvent-free battery electrode manufacturing , as well as several investments in Asia and the Americas, this expansion further strengthens a particularly dense global R&D network, that combines the expertise developed in France with that of the Group’s research centers in China, South Korea, Japan and the United States. Thanks to this international organization, Arkema is accelerating the development of innovative solutions capable of addressing the technological and industrial challenges of next- generation batteries.
Located at the heart of the Rhône-Alpes Research Center , the Battery Center of Excellence is entering a new phase of its development. Its footprint will be tripled, and its research infrastructure will be modernized, including notably a significant increase in the digitalization of R&D activities. This expansion will consolidate the role of this French center as Arkema’s global reference platform for the development of advanced materials serving both current batteries and the next generations under development.
The project will enable the Group’s R&D teams to prepare for the future industrial standards of cell manufacturers and accelerate the integration of Arkema’s advanced materials into their production processes. By replicating their customers’ manufacturing conditions, researchers will be able to better anticipate implementation constraints and contribute to the development of more efficient batteries delivering greater energy density, faster charging times and enhanced safety.
Armand Ajdari, Arkema’s Chief technology Officer: "This investment marks a major milestone in Arkema’s ambition to support the rapid evolution of the battery market. By strengthening our Battery Center of Excellence in France, we are equipping our global network and teams with state-of-the-art tools that will enable them to develop, in close collaboration with our customers, the materials that will contribute to the performance of tomorrow’s batteries."
The implementation of this project has been made possible in particular through the support provided by the French Research Tax Credit ( Crédit d’Impôt Recherche ) and by the French State as part of the France 2030 program.

Silicone Materials Target Battery Thermal Management and Assembly
By JJ Moore 
Image: IM Imagery
October 8, 2026
ANN ARBOR, Mich. — Wacker Chemical Corp. has introduced silicone materials designed to address thermal management, thermal runaway protection and assembly challenges in increasingly integrated battery packs.
ELASTOSIL CM 146 US A/B is a sprayable silicone coating that remains flexible after curing but forms a hard ceramic shield at temperatures above 600 C. The barrier provides thermal insulation intended to protect surrounding components during a thermal runaway event.
For battery potting applications, ELASTOSIL RT 7650 TC VS A/B is a low-viscosity, self-leveling silicone compound with customizable thermal conductivity ranging from 1.2 to 3.0 W/m·K. The two-part material provides primerless adhesion and is designed for efficient dispensing.
WACKER is also introducing SEMICOSIL PE 9351 TC VS A/B for battery and electronics assembly. The two-component hybrid adhesive provides thermal conductivity up to 2.0 W/m·K, non-slump dispensing, room-temperature curing and UL 94 V-0 flame-retardant performance. The material is designed to support increasingly integrated battery designs as manufacturers move from module-to-pack toward cell-to-pack architectures.
“Thermal management is closely connected to both battery performance and the manufacturing process,” said Peter Zorney, senior director of WACKER's Electronics and Automotive business segment for North and Central America. “Engineers have to consider how a material behaves during dispensing and curing, how it performs across operating temperatures and how effectively it supports the application over time while fulfilling increasingly demanding safety requirements.”
WACKER will display the materials at The Battery Show, Oct. 12-15 in Detroit.
