title: Bayer to invest 2.2 billion U.S. dollars in a new manufacturing site in the United States - Bayer
query: ("Bayer" OR "Bayer AG") ("press release" OR "investor relations" OR earnings OR announcement OR investment OR expansion OR acquisition OR partnership OR Korea) after:2026-10-01 before:2026-11-01
content_text:
Bayer to invest 2.2 billion U.S. dollars in a new manufacturing site in the United States
Summary
Company plans to build state-of-the-art site in New Albany, Ohio, U.S., to serve patients in the U.S. as well as globally / Bayer expects to create around 600 new high-value jobs in the area / Multi-year investment reinforces U.S. business expansion and adds to more than seven billion dollars in U.S. pharma R&D and manufacturing expenditure over past five years
New Albany, Ohio, U.S., October 2, 2026 – Bayer announced on Friday plans to invest 2.2 billion U.S. dollars in a new pharmaceutical manufacturing site in New Albany, Ohio, U.S. Building on more than seven billion dollars in U.S. pharma R&D and manufacturing spend over the past five years, the project is a central element of Bayer’s long-term growth strategy and commitment to innovation and patient access in its largest pharmaceuticals market. 
“Bayer has long seen the United States as a key manufacturing base and innovation hub. This landmark investment underscores our commitment,” said Bayer CEO Bill Anderson. “The new site will be home to manufacturing expertise and a skilled workforce that will strengthen our ability to deliver innovative, high-quality medicines to patients both in the United States and abroad.” 
“The United States is a key market for Bayer’s Pharmaceuticals division. This expansion is another important step to grow our pharmaceuticals business and to meet the demand of our customers and patients in the U.S., our fastest-growing pharmaceuticals market, and beyond,” said Sebastian Guth, Global Chief Operating Officer, Bayer Pharmaceuticals and President, Bayer U.S. 
Planned site to create highly-skilled jobs and support Ohio’s economic development 
Bayer is expected to create around 600 high-value jobs in the New Albany International Business Park and roughly 1,500 construction jobs during the facility’s construction. 
The flexible, modular campus is designed to combine drug substance and drug product manufacturing, leverage advanced digital and automation technologies, and support our growing portfolio initially in oncology, cardiovascular and renal care. The first module, dedicated to drug substance manufacturing, is expected to become operational in 2031. 
A second module for drug product manufacturing is planned to follow in 2034. The new site will complement Bayer’s U.S. pharmaceuticals headquarters in Whippany, New Jersey and its other sites in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania; Berkeley, California; Cambridge, Massachusetts; Research Triangle Park, North Carolina; and San Diego, California. 
“The facility will be a strong strategic addition to our global Product Supply network. As we continue to invest in our existing manufacturing sites around the globe, our planned presence in Ohio will further enhance our ability to serve our markets with greater resilience and reliability,” said Holger Weintritt, Head of Product Supply at Bayer’s Pharmaceuticals division. 
The site will also form part of a new U.S. based collaboration ecosystem. The ambition is to connect cutting-edge academic innovation with advanced manufacturing expertise to create a strong ecosystem that supports future-ready pharmaceutical production. 
About Bayer 
Bayer is a global enterprise with core competencies in the life science fields of health care and nutrition. Airbus, Kevin Piechota | Shutterstock, Simple Flying ""
data-is-feature-img="true"

By  
Daniel S Osipov 
Published Oct 2, 2026, 2:00 PM EDT 
Daniel comes to Simple Flying with a business focused approach to the aviation world. Daniel enjoys analyzing strategy and how companies move against each other to gain a step ahead in the skies. Besides strategy, Daniel also has a passion for aircraft design and the history of aviation.
Based in New York 
Sign in to your Simple Flying account
The Airbus A380 is in an interesting phase of its life today. The type received 251 orders by the time Airbus announced the program's end in 2019, while the COVID-19 pandemic saw operators ground either their entire A380 fleets or nearly all of them. In an era where worldwide passenger traffic fell by about 90%, a double-decker airliner with 500 seats and four engines was the wrong type of aircraft for essentially every airline. 
Add Simple Flying on Google 
Add as Preferred Source 
Follow on Google Discover 
However, in 2026, 189 A380s are still in service, or about 75% of the number delivered. For most A380 customers that returned the superjumbo to service, the parking of these birds was always intended to be temporary. However, there are some high-profile examples of airlines retiring their A380s fully before reversing course.
In part, this is because long-haul travel demand recovered much faster than airlines anticipated, while deliveries of new widebodies slowed. The Boeing 777-9 also continues to be delayed, but, today, the writing is on the wall for the A380, as the world's most capable twin-jet is now preparing to enter service.
Airbus A380 Operations Today
Credit: MC MEDIASTUDIO | Shutterstock 
The A380 is currently being flown worldwide by ten airlines: Emirates , British Airways , Singapore Airlines , Qantas , Etihad Airways , Lufthansa , Qatar Airways , Asiana Airlines , Korean Air , and All Nippon Airways . Of these ten, Emirates is by far the largest operator with 116 in its fleet, followed by British Airways and Singapore Airlines with 12 each. 
Meanwhile, All Nippon Airways is the smallest with just three examples, while the worldwide A380 fleet (including planes temporarily stored and parked that are set to re-enter service) amounts to 189. Four airlines permanently removed their A380s due to the pandemic: Air France, Hi Fly Malta (which acquired its sole A380 second-hand), Malaysia Airlines, and Thai Airways. Meanwhile, China Southern retired its double-deckers in 2022.
In addition, Emirates, Singapore Airlines, Qantas, Etihad Airways, Lufthansa, Qatar Airways, and Korean Air have all trimmed their fleets compared to before the pandemic, but are still operating the type, and not all of these carriers have announced retirement schedules. Asiana Airlines was planning to retire the A380 in 2026, but this timeline has been pushed back due to new aircraft delays .
Qantas aims to remove all of its A380s in 2028, and Korean Air intends to retire the A380 by 2031, while Lufthansa will start retiring the A380 after 2030. Unexpectedly, the A380 has made a comeback, and it will be sticking around well into the next decade. In part, this is because travel demand rose quite quickly, while new aircraft continue to arrive behind schedule, but there's one aircraft that has been particularly influential in keeping the A380 going.
Delays With The Boeing 777-9
Credit: EQRoy I Shutterstock 
Among the ten current operators of the A380, only two (Asiana Airlines and Qantas) have yet to order the Boeing 777-9. Asiana is merging with Korean Air, which has ordered the 777-9, and so it's really Qantas that has abstained from buying Boeing's upcoming giant, as it's favoring the Airbus A350-1000 instead.
The aircraft was originally set to enter service in 2020, but it's now been delayed until 2027, and the 777-9's development has taken nearly as long as Concorde. Most 777-9 customers didn't order the aircraft to replace the A380 specifically, especially given that most of these double-deckers are fairly young .

However, had the plane arrived on time, there would have been dozens in service already, and you would see existing customers begin considering 777-9s as A380 replacements, given how much more economical it is. As such, with a seven-year delay and more uncertainty still about actual delivery timelines, airlines have had to reinvest in their A380s for the time being.
Lufthansa, which intends to use the 777-9 as a Boeing 747-400 replacement first, is now updating the business class cabin on its A380s and will keep them until the next decade. Had the 777-9s come on time, the 747-400s would have already been gone, while the A380s likely wouldn't have gotten new interiors. Emirates planned to have received over 100 777-9s by 2026, as per its original contract, but it's now refurbishing its A380s while it has yet to fly a single 777-9.
Threats To The A380's Survival
Credit: Airbus 
Airbus is working to certify the A350-1000ULR, which could be the final nail in the A380's coffin. It's not necessarily because of the plane itself, since Qantas is the only customer for the type, but it's more about what the A350-1000ULR represents . The A380 is fundamentally designed for routes between major airline hubs and large spokes.
Meanwhile, planes like the Boeing 787 and Airbus A350 are designed to serve smaller cities nonstop, in what's been commonly referred to as the 'point-to-point' model. The A350-1000ULR is far from being a small aircraft, but the main benefit of the aircraft is that it has the longest range of any airliner in production today.
Qantas will use this plane to connect Sydney to London and New York, all three of which are huge cities, but which were too far apart to be connected nonstop until now. Once the airline begins operating these routes, it'll have less need to operate A380s on its trunk routes to destinations such as Los Angeles and Dallas/Fort Worth. Qantas carries a substantial amount of connecting passengers on these routes.
Furthermore, by flying to more destinations nonstop, the airline doesn't require so much capacity on its trunk routes. The A350-1000ULR represents the final evolution of the point-to-point model, even if it's connecting Sydney to two of the world's largest cities , and airlines are continuing to take massive numbers of Boeing 787s and Airbus A350s to implement this concept on a wider scale. This is reducing the need to operate the A380.
The Current Challenges Facing The A380
Credit: photojohn830 I Shutterstock 
The A380 has extremely high operating costs, and this means that airlines need to sell almost all of the aircraft's seats to make a profit. The aircraft can work on routes like London to Los Angeles or Singapore to Sydney, and it can actually prove quite lucrative as well. However, jet fuel prices are currently elevated due to the war in Iran, which has narrowed the gap considerably between operating costs and revenue.
For the A380, which already has immense operating costs, this makes the economics extremely difficult. Qantas originally planned to begin retiring its A380s in 2032, with future orders expected to be placed for their replacements. The A350s and 787s that the airline currently has on order would be used for growth and to start replacing Qantas' Airbus A330 fleet.
However, the carrier recently announced that it was moving the retirement timeline for the A380 fleet a full four years (up to 2028) , and that all ten examples that Qantas currently flies would be gone by the middle of the year. Qantas operates the A380 on some of the world's longest routes, and it's feeling the pain of higher fuel prices even more than most other A380 operators .
Considering that airlines have generally been pushing back their A380 retirement dates, it was an unexpected announcement from Qantas, and it's clear that elevated oil prices have changed the economics of flying the superjumbo. Whether this will push other carriers to put their A380s out to pasture remains to be seen.
Who's Committed To The A380 For The Long Run?
Credit: Wangkun Jia I Shutterstock 
One of the most useful ways to determine an airline's commitment to a fleet is interior refurbishments. While they don't guarantee that an aircraft will remain with an airline long-term, carriers typically need to use the plane for several years afterward to justify the investment, and interior retrofit projects for an A380 can cost tens of millions per aircraft. Lufthansa, for example, is currently retrofitting its A380s with new business class seats.
However, it will not use the full Allegris cabins that are being rolled out to the rest of the fleet. Still it intends to keep its examples flying until the 2030s. British Airways, meanwhile, is committing to a full nose-to-tail retrofit of all 12 A380s in its fleet, including new seats in all four travel classes and a new layout that will feature the world's largest business class cabin . Elsewhere, Emirates is refurbishing its A380s with premium economy and intends to install the cabin on 110 A380s out of the 116 it currently uses.
Emirates and British Airways are committed to the A380, while Qantas and Korean Air will retire the type within the next several years. Lufthansa will follow shortly in the 2030s, while Qatar Airways' and Singapore Airlines' long-term intentions for the A380 remain to be seen. However, another interesting case to monitor is Etihad Airways.
Although the Abu Dhabi-based carrier hasn't been refurbishing its A380s, it is currently working on returning its ninth A380 to service, with that aircraft expected to begin flying passengers again in January 2027 . Returning previously stored aircraft to service is also an expensive process, and the fact that Etihad is continuing to do this signals that it sees a long-term place within its fleet for the A380.

content_text:
James Gunn & Peter Safran To Stay At DC Studios After Paramount-Warner Bros Merger
By Anthony D'Alessandro 
Anthony D'Alessandro 
Editorial Director/Box Office Editor
@AwardsTony 
More Stories By Anthony

2026 Worldwide Box Office Headed To Near $36B, Best Since 2019

Story Arc 
L-R: James Gunn and Peter Safran 
Getty Images 
James Gunn and Peter Safran , the bosses of Warner Bros-owned label DC Studios , will continue to lead the film, TV and comic book production hub and do what they do best after Paramount closes its acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery.
Once upon a time, the Marvel Cinematic Universe was in Paramount’s hands, having a distribution deal with the comic-book label and launching the megaverse with Iron Man, Thor, Captain America and Iron Man 2. Then Marvel took a hike to Disney, which scooped them up for $4 billion in 2009. With DC, Paramount no doubt gains a massive franchise one-up in its library that already includes Star Trek, Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, and Mission: Impossible. 
Related Stories 
Executives
Josh Greenstein & Dana Goldberg Poised To Run Combined Paramount Warner Bros Film Unit, Setting Up Likely Michael De Luca & Pamela Abdy Exit 
News
Paramount-WBD Will Now Be Called Skydance, David Ellison Reveals 
We hear the duo had a recent meeting with new Skydance co-CEO David Ellison about their future and it went well. Per this morning’s news, all film units, Paramount and Warner Bros, are to report into Paramount Pictures co-chairs Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein . The future of Warner Bros motion picture chairs Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy remains up in the air at the newly relabeled Skydance entertainment conglomerate; that duo is still in need of a chat with Ellison.
Watch on Deadline 
Gunn has been shooting the Superman sequel Man of Tomorrow, set for release on July 9, 2027. The label’s Clayface, about the Batman antagonist, is their first lower-budget genre movie, opens October 23. Warner Bros’ second highest-grossing movie last year was Gunn’s Superman with more than $618 million at the global box office. Also in production at DC is Matt Reeves’ sequel The Batman Part II set for February 18, 2028. This past summer’s Supergirl didn’t go so well, with a global gross of $126.4M.
Meanwhile, the DC-HBO Max series Lanterns has been a ratings success. Co-created by Tom King, Damon Lindelof and Chris Mundy, it saw its third episode score a massive 10M global viewers in its first three days — 7M from the U.S. Since Lanterns premiered August 16, the pilot has been seen by more than 20 million viewers worldwide and continues to grow, the company said. The series launched as one of HBO Max’s top titles .
Safran and Gunn were appointed to lead DC Studios in October 2022 in a new label strategy orchestrated by WBD CEO David Zaslav to mimic Disney’s production label hub structure of Marvel Studios, Lucasfilm, Pixar, etc., with myriad production heads. It was arguably the first time (unless we count Charlie Chaplin) that a filmmaker, Gunn, did double duty as a studio executive.
Safran already had a hot streak at Warners/New Line with the multibillion-dollar The Conjuring franchise and also producing DC franchise titles like Shazam and Aquaman . Safran had produced on Gunn’s 2021 The Suicide Squad movie and its HBO Max spinoff series Peacemaker starring John Cena, which has clocked two seasons.
This is all according to sources Friday morning. Paramount and DC couldn’t be reached for comment.

Samsung Fire & Marine Insurance Trains with Toray Arrows in Japan
[OSEN=Cho Hyung-rae Reporter] Daejeon Samsung Fire & Marine Insurance BlueFangs, a professional volleyball team, will conduct a training camp in Japan to finalize preparations for the upcoming season.
Samsung Fire & Marine Insurance will travel to Shizuoka, Japan, on October 2, conduct joint training and matches with Toray Arrows, and is scheduled to return on the 7th.
Ahead of the 2026-2027 season, Samsung Fire & Marine Insurance appointed Tommi Tiilikainen as head coach to improve the team’s structure. This marks the club’s first foreign coach. Tiilikainen previously led Korean Air to three consecutive combined championships from the 2021-2022 season.
During the off-season, Samsung Fire & Marine Insurance attempted to transition to the fast and organic playstyle advocated by Coach Tommi. Through this training, the team plans to evaluate the results of their preparations and gear up for the 2026-2027 season.
A source from Samsung Fire & Marine Insurance BlueFangs stated, “The players trained extremely hard during the off-season. This will be a great opportunity to test their progress against a high-level Japanese professional team and learn from them.”

content_text:
Vestas Powers Up Vietnam's Clean Energy Ambitions with Two New Wind Projects
Friday, 02 October 2026 
REM 
Vestas has been awarded contracts to supply its 16 new V163 wind turbines from the 4 MW Platform across two new wind farms in central Vietnam. In partnership with a Vietnamese renewable energy developer with a significant portfolio, Vestas will expand proven track record of 1.6 gigawatts in Vietnam and strengthen the company's role in driving the country's wind energy growth. Vestas Asia Pacific 
Included in Vietnam's Power Development Plan 8 (PDP8), these projects are among the first to secure investment licenses and proceed toward execution, supporting the country's clean energy transition and its pathway toward net-zero emissions by 2050. The awards highlight growing momentum in Vietnam's wind sector and demonstrate how advanced turbine technology can help unlock the next generation of projects under PDP8. Through higher hub heights, larger rotors and site-specific solutions, Vestas is helping developers improve project economics and maximise energy production in Vietnam's wind conditions.
The 163 metre rotors will be the largest Vestas model deployed in Vietnam to date. Combined with tailor-made 155-meter hub height tower solutions, they are designed to maximise energy production and project performance for Vietnam's wind conditions.
Built on Vestas' proven 4 MW platform, which already accounts for +88 GW of installed capacity globally and 1.6 GW of installed capacity in Vietnam, the solution combines increased energy yield with demonstrated operational performance and track record in the market. The projects will also be backed by 20-year AOM 5000 service and maintenance agreements, delivering long-term business case certainty and optimal operational performance.
"We are honored by our customer's confidence and proud to be supporting some of the first wind projects moving forward under PDP8. These projects demonstrate that the next generation of wind development in Vietnam can be enabled through innovative, proven technology and tailor-made solutions.
"With our V163-4 MW platform, 155-meter site specific hub height configuration and deep local expertise, Vestas is delivering a solution specifically designed for Vietnam's evolving market needs. We remain committed to supporting the country's energy security and helping our customers accelerate Vietnam's clean energy transition , " Antoine CROIZE, Country Manager, Vestas Vietnam.
Vestas Backs Vietnam's Local Employment 
The two wind farms will be located near an existing hub of Vestas projects, extending long-term service employment in the region for decades to come.
Vestas' wind turbine components are expected to begin delivery to Vietnam in 2027, with commissioning to follow.

Onsemi agrees to buy Synaptics for $123/share in cash in revised deal
1 min read 
ON SYNA 
Onsemi ON announced a new agreement to acquire Synaptics SYNA for $123 a share in cash, revising an all-stock deal that was disclosed in June. The amended agreement came after an unsolicited competing proposal. 
Shares of Synaptics jumped 13% in after-hours trading, while onsemi rose 5.2%. 
Under the revised agreement, onsemi will acquire Synaptics SYNA for $123 a share in cash for an aggregate value of approximately $5.7 billion as compared to ~$7 billion for the prior agreement, according to a statement on Thursday. The deal is expected to be immediately accretive to onsemi's non-GAAP earnings per share. 
“As was the case when we initially announced the acquisition, Synaptics addresses an important aspect of our strategic direction, and we believe the revised merger agreement represents a more financially attractive transaction for our shareholders,” said Hassane El-Khoury, president and CEO of onsemi, in the statement. 
After review with its financial and legal advisors, the Synaptics board SYNA unanimously determined that the onsemi transaction, as amended, continues to be in the best interests of Synaptics and its shareholders. 
“By transitioning to an all-cash structure, we are providing value certainty at a meaningful premium as compared to current value," Synaptics CEO Rahul Patel said in the joint statement. "We are confident this path is the right choice for our shareholders." 
The deal will be financed through a combination of cash on hand and committed financing. Onsemi has obtained fully committed debt financing from Morgan Stanley. The amended merger agreement does not include a closing condition related to onsemi’s financing. The transaction is still expected to close by mid-2027. Arkema expands battery Center of Excellence in France with €10 million investment
October 1, 2026 | By Mary Bailey 
Arkema S.A. (Colombes, France) is continuing to invest in the battery value chain and recently announced a €10 million expansion project for its Global Battery Center of Excellence located in Oullins-Pierre-Bénite, in the Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes region of France.
This investment reflects the Group’s strategy of continuously strengthening its research capabilities in advanced materials for batteries within its global network of R&D laboratories covering the entire battery value chain.
Following the inauguration in Normandy in September 2025 of a laboratory dedicated to solvent-free battery electrode manufacturing , as well as several investments in Asia and the Americas, this expansion further strengthens a particularly dense global R&D network that combines the expertise developed in France with that of the Group’s research centers in China, South Korea, Japan, and the United States. Thanks to this international organization, Arkema (Colombes, France) is accelerating the development of innovative solutions capable of addressing the technological and industrial challenges of next-generation batteries .
Located at the heart of the Rhône-Alpes Research Center, the Battery Center of Excellence is entering a new phase of its development. Its footprint will be tripled and its research infrastructure will be modernized, including notably a significant increase in the digitalization of R&D activities. This expansion will consolidate the role of this French center as Arkema’s global reference platform for the development of advanced materials serving both current batteries and the next generations under development.
The project will enable the Group’s R&D teams to prepare for the future industrial standards of cell manufacturers and accelerate the integration of Arkema’s advanced materials into their production processes. By replicating their customers’ manufacturing conditions, researchers will be able to better anticipate implementation constraints and contribute to the development of more efficient batteries delivering greater energy density, faster charging times, and enhanced safety.
“This investment marks a major milestone in Arkema’s ambition to support the rapid evolution of the battery market. By strengthening our Battery Center of Excellence in France, we are equipping our global network and teams with state-of-the-art tools that will enable them to develop, in close collaboration with our customers, the materials that will contribute to the performance of tomorrow’s batteries.” — Armand Ajdari, Arkema’s Chief Technology Officer.

ABL Texcell Diagnostics Raises Its 2026 Revenue Guidance to €13.5 Million - €14.0 Million
Business Wire 
October 1, 2026 7 min read 
ABNX.PA 
ABLD.PA 
Revised guidance includes the expected contribution from TEXCELL activities since their acquisition in the second half of 2026 
Revised 2026 revenue guidance of €13.5 million to €14.0 million, compared with the €12.265 million target announced on 1 June 2026, representing an increase of 10.1% to 14.1%. 
Corresponding year-on-year growth of 94.2% to 101.4% compared with 2025 revenue of €6.950 million. 
First-half 2026 results: revenue of €5.415 million (+90.0%), EBITDA of €1.315 million and EBITDA margin of 24.3%. 
Integration of TEXCELL activities, first publicly announced partnership with ABIONYX Pharma and rollout of an expanded offering across molecular diagnostics, virology and life sciences. 
WOIPPY, France, October 01, 2026 --( BUSINESS WIRE )--Regulatory News: 
ABL Texcell Diagnostics (Euronext Paris: ABLD – ISIN: FR001400AHX6) (the "Company"), a company specializing in molecular diagnostic solutions, healthcare software and services supporting clinical research, s raising its revenue guidance for the financial year ending 31 December 2026. Based on the commercial, operational and accounting information available as of the date of this press release, the Company now expects revenue to be between €13.5 million and €14.0 million. 
This revised range updates the €12.265 million revenue target announced on 1 June 2026. It reflects first-half performance, business activity observed since the beginning of the second half of the year and the expected contribution from the TEXCELL activities and assets since their acquisition. It represents the best estimate available as of the date of this press release and does not constitute guidance for operating profit, EBITDA or net profit for the 2026 financial year. 
1. 2026 REVENUE GUIDANCE RAISED TO €13.5 MILLION - €14.0 MILLION 
On 1 June 2026, the Company announced a full-year revenue target of €12.265 million, representing targeted growth of 76.5% compared with the €6.950 million achieved in 2025. The revised range represents an increase of €1.235 million to €1.735 million, or 10.1% to 14.1%, compared with the initial target. 
Compared with 2025 revenue, the revised guidance represents year-on-year growth of 94.2% to 101.4%.

Story Continues 
2. FIRST-HALF 2026 PERFORMANCE SUPPORTS THE REVISED OUTLOOK 
As of 30 June 2026, ABL Diagnostics had generated revenue of €5.415 million, compared with €2.849 million in the first half of 2025, representing reported growth of 90.0%. EBITDA amounted to €1.315 million, compared with €0.295 million a year earlier, bringing the EBITDA margin to 24.3%. EBIT reached €1.115 million and net profit amounted to €1.280 million. 
These results, published on 8 September 2026 and subsequently detailed in the 2026 Half-Year Financial Report made available on 30 September 2026, confirmed the acceleration of the Company's historical businesses and the growing contribution from its new growth drivers. 
First-half revenue represented 44.2% of the then-current full-year revenue target of €12.265 million. This comparison is purely arithmetic and should not be regarded as an extrapolation of second-half performance. 
3. TEXCELL EXPANDS THE GROUP'S SCOPE FROM THE SECOND HALF OF 2026 
On 21 July 2026, the Évry Commercial Court selected ABL Diagnostics to acquire the activities and assets of TEXCELL. The transaction includes, in particular, the continuation of operations at the Genopole site in Évry-Courcouronnes, the acquisition of the transferred assets and contracts and the integration of 29 employees, including 23 employees under permanent employment contracts and six apprentices. 
TEXCELL brings expertise in viral safety and viral clearance, biosafety, virology, cell culture, genomic analysis, immunomonitoring and services for biotechnology and pharmaceutical companies. The contribution included in the revised guidance relates solely to the acquired activities from their effective date of transfer to the Company and excludes any activities performed prior to the acquisition. 
Work relating to the definitive scope of certain transferred contracts, the allocation of ongoing services and the accounting recognition of related revenue remains in progress. Their final impact will be determined as part of the Company's year-end closing procedures. 
4. FIRST COMMERCIAL MILESTONES AND SYNERGIES 
On 10 September 2026, the TEXCELL division announced that it had been selected by ABIONYX Pharma to conduct viral safety and viral clearance studies in connection with the preparation of process validation batches for CER-001. This collaboration represents the first publicly announced example, since the acquisition, of TEXCELL's ability to support biopharmaceutical programmes at key industrial and regulatory stages. 
At the same time, the Company's existing businesses continue to benefit from the growing contribution of UltraGene, DeepChek genotyping and sequencing solutions, healthcare software, and distribution and service activities. The cooperation with CDL Pharma also forms part of this momentum, notably through the international multi-year agreement announced on 11 June 2026, with a potential value of approximately €2.7 million through 2031, with revenue recognized as the related services are effectively performed. 
The combination of these activities expands the Company's addressable market and creates cross-selling opportunities across molecular diagnostics, genomic analysis, clinical research and viral safety. At this stage, however, the Company does not separately quantify the future impact of these synergies beyond the revenue already reflected in its 2026 guidance range. 
5. ABL TEXCELL DIAGNOSTICS: AN IDENTITY ALIGNED WITH THE COMPANY'S EXPANDED SCOPE 
On 17 September 2026, shareholders convened in an Extraordinary General Meeting approved the Company's new corporate name, ABL Texcell Diagnostics. This new identity reflects the growing complementarity between the Company's molecular diagnostics, virology and life sciences activities. Shareholders also resolved to maintain the listing of the Company's shares on the regulated market of Euronext Paris. 
The Company intends to continue the operational and commercial integration of TEXCELL, secure the transferred contracts, develop cross-selling opportunities and execute the industrial, scientific and technological investments required to support its development. 
FORWARD-LOOKING STATEMENTS (SAFE HARBOR) 
This press release contains forward-looking statements, including 2026 revenue guidance of between €13.5 million and €14.0 million. These statements are based on the commercial, operational and accounting information available as of the date of publication and on assumptions that the Company considers reasonable as of that date. 
Actual results may differ from these estimates, in particular as a result of the timing and level of contract execution, the performance, invoicing and accounting recognition of services, adjustments relating to the acquisition of the TEXCELL activities, year-end closing procedures, changes in market conditions, supply-chain developments and regulatory requirements. The Company will update forward-looking information, where required, in accordance with applicable legal and regulatory requirements. 
The final results for the 2026 financial year will be approved by the competent corporate bodies and will be subject to the applicable review and publication procedures.

TOPICS: and private and business aviation markets. The entry into service of the helicopter is planned in 2028 for the emergency medical services segment. The H140 features a wide range of innovations powered by CFM International’s new generation power plant Safran 
Posted By: Aeromorning

Safran Doubles Texas Missile-Engine Capacity as Western Defence Production Accelerates
AeroMorning John Smith October 1, 2026
Driven by NATO rearmament, the war in Ukraine, and surging demand for long-range strike and anti-ship capabilities, Western defence industries are shifting from low-volume peacetime manufacturing toward a significantly higher-volume industrial model.
1. Safran’s Texas Expansion and the TR40 Engine 
The Investment: On September 30, 2026, Safran announced that its subsidiary, Safran Power Units, headquartered in Toulouse with U.S. operations, will double the capacity of its Grand Prairie, Texas, facility . A new U.S. assembly line dedicated to the TR40 engine family will come online in 2028.
TR40 Metrics: Demand for the TR40 has quadrupled in recent years. More than 1,200 engines have been delivered worldwide, making it Safran Power Units’ best-selling turbojet product. Safran describes the company as the European leader in turbojets for missiles and target drones.
Role: The compact, reliable turbojet, with a high thrust-to-weight ratio, sits at the heart of two major European anti-ship missile programmes: Kongsberg’s NSM and MBDA’s Exocet Block III. Originally developed as the Microturbo TR40, it powered the NSM’s first flight in 2005, before Microturbo became part of Safran, and the Exocet Block III’s first flight in 2006.
2. Kongsberg’s Naval Strike Missile (NSM) 
Capabilities & Deployment: Developed by Norway’s Kongsberg Defence & Aerospace, the NSM is a low-altitude anti-ship and land-attack missile designed for high survivability. It can be launched from ships and mobile coastal-defence systems and is deployed by the U.S. Navy on Littoral Combat Ships and Constellation-class frigates, as well as by the U.S. Marine Corps.
U.S. Industrial Partnership: For the U.S. programme, Kongsberg partnered with Raytheon, now RTX , the U.S. prime contractor. Raytheon manufactures NSM launchers, missiles and components in the United States, including final assembly and testing at its Tucson, Arizona facility. Kongsberg remains the NSM’s developer and principal manufacturer. As demand grows, Kongsberg is also establishing a U.S. manufacturing and sustainment facility in Virginia, adding capacity to the American industrial base alongside RTX rather than replacing its role.
Global Adoption: Entering Norwegian service in 2012, Denmark became the 14th country to select the NSM in March 2025, joining Norway, Poland, Malaysia, Germany, the U.S., Romania, Canada, Australia, Spain, the U.K., the Netherlands, Belgium and Latvia. The programme also has an air-launched derivative, the Joint Strike Missile (JSM).
Contracts & Financials: In November 2024, Kongsberg signed its largest missile contract ever with the U.S. Navy, worth NOK 10 billion (approximately US$900 million), with options taking the value to NOK 12 billion (approximately US$1.1 billion). Its Missiles & Aerostructures division’s revenue jumped approximately 63%, from US$570 million in 2023 to US$930 million in 2025, while its order backlog grew approximately 54%, from US$3.7 billion to US$5.7 billion.
Industrial Scale: Kongsberg is expanding production globally through a new factory in Norway, a developing facility in Australia, and its Virginia plant, scheduled to begin manufacturing in late 2027 and reach full-rate production by late 2028.
3. MBDA’s Exocet and the Wider Industrial Boom 
Exocet Lineage: Owned by Airbus, BAE Systems and Leonardo, MBDA produces the Exocet family, with ship-, air- and submarine-launched variants. At Euronaval 2024, MBDA marked its 4,000th Exocet produced, making it one of the most extensively produced Western anti-ship missile families.
MM40 Block 3C: The latest generation offers a 250-km-class operational range, a new-generation seeker and improved guidance designed to operate in all weather and withstand electronic warfare and countermeasures.
MBDA Production Surge: Overall missile production doubled between 2023 and the end of 2025, with another 40% increase planned for 2026. MBDA is investing 205 billion in Europe between 2026 and 2030, twice its previous plan, and expects to hire 2,800 people in 2026.

Rauschenberger leaves Siemens Energy’s investment arm 
Oct 1, 2026 • Oishani Mitra 
Kendra Rauschenberger has taken on the role of vice president of global sales for onshore wind at Siemens Gamesa. 
Kendra Rauschenberger has left her position as general partner at Siemens Energy Ventures, the corporate VC arm of German energy technology company Siemens Energy, after six and a half years to take on the role of vice president of global sales for onshore wind at Siemens Gamesa.
A GCV Powerlister , Rauschenberger was one of the founding members of Siemens Energy Ventures and played a role growing the unit into “a platform across venture building, venture clienting and venture capital capabilities that is delivering impact and is now embedded in how Siemens Energy approaches innovation and solves business challenges”.
The move to Siemens Gamesa marks a return to wind power for Rauschenberger, who started her journey there when she joined Siemens Energy in 2000 as a trainee.
“I am excited to join the Onshore Wind team at a time when our industry is evolving rapidly and the demand for clean, reliable and affordable energy has never been greater. I look forward to learning and building the future together with colleagues, customers and partners around the world as we help shape the future of energy,” she said in the LinkedIn post announcing her move.
Siemens Energy Ventures was launched in 2020 and works with cleantech startups through venture capital, partnerships, venture building and venture clienting.

Applied Materials and Besi Expand AI Advanced Packaging Partnership Through EPIC Center
Fiona Craig 
October 1, 2026 3 min read 
AMAT 
-7.49% 
Artificial intelligence applications ©Shutterstock The expanded collaboration moves beyond hybrid bonding into 3D IC integration, thermo-compression bonding, panel-scale packaging and photonics technologies designed to support AI system scaling. 
Key Investor Takeaways 
Applied Materials (NASDAQ:AMAT) and Besi (EU:BESI) are expanding their AI advanced packaging partnership, with Besi becoming an Innovation Partner at Applied's EPIC Center. 
The companies will broaden joint development beyond hybrid bonding into 3D IC scaling, thermo-compression bonding, die-on-panel integration and photonics-enabled interconnects. 
The partnership targets higher-density and higher-bandwidth connections required for increasingly complex AI compute and memory architectures. 
Besi engineers will work alongside Applied teams at the EPIC Center, potentially giving mutual customers earlier access to jointly developed packaging processes. 
Applied expects capital spending on its new Silicon Valley EPIC Center to scale over time to approximately $5 billion as customer projects begin. 
Why AMAT Stock Is in Focus 
Applied Materials is expanding its semiconductor packaging collaboration with Besi as AI infrastructure increases requirements for higher-density chip interconnects. 
Besi will join Applied's EPIC Center as an Innovation Partner, extending a relationship that began with a joint development programme in 2020. The companies previously established a Center of Excellence in Singapore that combined Applied's semiconductor process technologies with Besi's die placement and assembly capabilities. 
That work produced Kinex, which the companies describe as the industry's first integrated die-to-wafer hybrid bonding system. 
The expanded programme will cover a wider portion of the advanced packaging process. Planned R&D includes new die-to-wafer hybrid bonding platforms, scaling of thermo-compression bonding, die-on-wafer, die-on-die and die-on-panel integration, and photonics-enabled interconnects for co-packaged optics and AI systems. 
The work is expected to focus particularly on next-generation 3D IC scaling and integration between logic and memory. 
Why This Matters for Investors 
The partnership positions advanced packaging as a larger part of Applied Materials' AI-related technology roadmap. As AI systems require increasingly close integration between compute, memory and other components, the manufacturing challenge extends beyond producing individual chips to connecting them efficiently within larger systems. 
Expanding the Besi partnership may allow Applied to address more of that integration process by combining its materials engineering and wafer-processing expertise with Besi's assembly and bonding technologies. 
Story Continues 
The collaboration could also shorten development cycles by bringing the two companies' engineers together with logic, memory and systems companies at the EPIC Center. According to Applied, the facility is intended to reduce the time required to move semiconductor technologies from early research into high-volume manufacturing. 
For investors, the announcement does not provide new revenue targets or financial guidance. Its significance instead lies in the companies broadening an existing technology partnership as advanced packaging becomes increasingly important to AI compute scaling. 
What to Watch Next 
Key developments will include the start of R&D programmes at the EPIC Center and progress toward new hybrid bonding, TCB, panel-level and photonics integration platforms. 
Investors can also watch for evidence that jointly developed technologies move from research into customer qualification and high-volume manufacturing, particularly as Applied's EPIC Center becomes operationally ready this year.

Asahi Kasei wraps years of global dealmaking into a single brand
By
Nick Paul Taylor 
Oct 1, 2026 7:16am 
Asahi Kasei 
Asahi Kasei Pharma 
AiCuris 
Veloxis 
Asahi is seeking deals to expand its pipeline and support continued growth. (Asahi Kasei )
After years of deal-driven global expansion, Asahi Kasei is rolling its pharma units up under a single brand and forging ahead with efforts to drive sales toward $2 billion by the end of the decade.
Tokyo-based Asahi has expanded globally through deals since 2020, when it put down roots in the U.S. by acquiring Veloxis Pharmaceuticals. In 2024, Asahi added Sweden’s Calliditas to its roster in a $1 billion deal. The conglomerate returned to the deal table in February, when it agreed to buy Germany’s Aicuris for about $920 million. 
The acquired biotechs retained their own branding—until now. Going forward, the units will all operate as Asahi Kasei Therapeutics, the name of the company’s existing Japanese pharma business. Integration establishes a unified global management structure for the pharmaceutical business, Asahi said. 
Bringing the units under a single global management structure “will allow us to make resource allocation decisions across the business rather than by company or geography,” Yoshikazu Aoki, global president of Asahi Kasei Therapeutics, said in a statement. Aoki added that the new structure provides “a stronger platform to pursue in-licensing opportunities.” 
Asahi is seeking deals to expand its pipeline and support continued growth. The company plans to invest about 40 billion Japanese yen ($250 million) in in-licensing over the next three years. In-licensing and additional M&A form part of Asahi’s strategy for growing revenues to 300 billion Japanese yen ($1.9 billion) by its 2030 financial year. 
The company focuses on specialty therapeutic areas, including immunology, nephrology, transplantation and infectious diseases. Asahi acquired the kidney transplant drug Envarsus XR in the Veloxis takeover. The company entered another kidney indication by acquiring Calliditas, which sells the immunoglobulin A nephropathy drug Tarpeyo. 
Buying Aicuris moved Asahi into infectious disease drug development. Aicuris receives royalties on sales of Prevymis, a cytomegalovirus drug licensed by Merck & Co., and has a pipeline of programs targeting infectious diseases, including herpes simplex virus.

The Experience Center Race: What Global Life Science Suppliers Are Really Building in India
October 01, 2026 | Thursday | Features | By Mansi Jamsudkar Padvekar
India's life sciences industry is entering a phase where global technology suppliers are competing on more than instruments and specifications. As pharmaceutical and biopharma companies move towards biologics, cell and gene therapies, advanced analytics and global-scale manufacturing, suppliers are investing in experience centres, application laboratories, bioprocessing hubs and R&D facilities closer to customers. Agilent Technologies' new Customer Experience Center in Mumbai is the latest example, following investments by Thermo Fisher Scientific, Cytiva and Merck Life Science across key Indian clusters. These facilities are becoming strategic assets—helping customers test technologies, solve process challenges and build skills, while giving suppliers a deeper role in the technology and workflow decisions shaping India's next phase of life sciences growth.
In April 2026, Agilent Technologies inaugurated its Customer Experience Center (CEC) in Mumbai, bringing together hands-on technology demonstrations, application expertise, and commercial operations under one roof. The facility complements Agilent's expanding India footprint, which already includes its India Solution Center in Manesar, a Refurbishment Center, and the Hyderabad Biopharma Experience Center, a connected network designed to support laboratories across pharmaceuticals, biotechnology, diagnostics, food safety, and environmental testing. Agilent is not acting alone. Over the past 18 months, several major global life sciences suppliers have opened, expanded, or announced experience, training, R&D and process-development facilities in India. The pattern points to a broader shift in strategy: suppliers are no longer competing on instrument specifications alone; they are increasingly competing on the depth of technical capability they can build around their technologies. 
Beyond sales: building local capabilities 
Agilent's Mumbai launch sits inside a much broader wave. Thermo Fisher Scientific inaugurated two facilities in Hyderabad's Genome Valley in November 2025, a Customer Experience Center (CEC) and a Bioprocess Design Center (BDC), representing an investment of Rs 90 crore, built in partnership with the Telangana government and India's Department of Biotechnology under the Biotech Park Project. The Hyderabad CEC alone demonstrates more than 50 integrated workflows across over 20 applications, spanning cell and gene therapy, mRNA, oncology, proteomics, and analytical sciences. 
"Thermo Fisher supports innovators as they move from scientific discovery to robust, scalable and commercially viable processes. Our CEC and BDC in Hyderabad advance this objective through three areas: access to advanced technologies, scientific collaboration for process development, talent development and industry–academia partnerships," said Srinath Venkatesh, Managing Director, India & South Asia, Thermo Fisher Scientific . "The centers bring research, analytical and bioprocessing capabilities together within a common environment, giving scientists and manufacturers access to integrated workflows across targeted therapeutics, multi-omics and translational research, bioprocessing design and manufacturing, equivalence studies and process monitoring. Hands-on training programmes are designed to build skills of scientists in research, QC & manufacturing to accelerate development and improve reproducibility & precision in these areas." 
Venkatesh pointed to a specific gap the centers are designed to close: "A challenge scientists and business face is translating research into robust, scalable and reproducible processes to shorten the path from discovery to clinical development and commercial manufacturing. At CEC and BDC, we partner with biopharma researchers and manufacturers on method development, optimisation, validation and proof-of-concept studies. This enables scientists to refine analytical workflows, improve reproducibility, and generate high-quality data that supports confident decision-making. In doing so, we can help organisations address development risks, improve productivity and accelerate the path from discovery through clinical development and commercial manufacturing." 
He also tied the centers to a longer-term talent strategy: "Building a strong biopharma ecosystem also requires a sustained focus on talent. Our industry–academia collaborations provide students and researchers with access to advanced technologies, hands-on training, certification programmes and continuing education aligned with industry requirements. Through internships, applied research projects and mentorship, we aim to strengthen the connection between academic learning and industry practice. Together, these initiatives are designed to build a future-ready scientific workforce, strengthen translational research and support India's continued growth as a globally competitive biopharma innovation and manufacturing hub." 
That distinction matters because India's next phase of life-sciences growth will require more than additional laboratory capacity. As biologics, cell and gene therapies, mRNA platforms and complex analytical workflows move towards commercial scale, suppliers increasingly need to be embedded in the development and manufacturing process itself. Experience centres therefore become more than demonstration facilities: they become points where technology adoption, process development and workforce training converge. 
Cytiva, the bioprocessing arm of Danaher Corporation, has been building out India capacity even more aggressively. In February-March 2026, it opened a 30,000-square-foot Fast Trak bioprocessing centre in Bengaluru, equipped with single-use bioreactor systems scaling up to 200 litres and ISO-certified validation labs. This followed an earlier expansion in Pune, a 33,000-square-foot manufacturing facility and Experience Center at Hinjawadi Rajiv Gandhi Infotech Park that doubled Cytiva's India manufacturing capacity and added immersive training programmes for upstream and downstream bioprocessing technologies. 
"We see India entering a new chapter in bioprocessing. The conversation is no longer just about manufacturing for India; it is increasingly about manufacturing from India for the world," said Manoj Kumar R Panicker, General Manager, South Asia at Cytiva . 
"As customers invest in biologics, biosimilars and CDMO-led growth, they need partners that can combine local supply, global technology and technical expertise. Expanding our Pune manufacturing capacity is a reflection of our long-term belief in India's role as a strategic biomanufacturing hub. Together with our Bengaluru Fast Trak and R&D capabilities, we are helping build the ecosystem that can accelerate innovation, scale and global competitiveness." 
Panicker also pointed to what he called a substantive basis for India's optimism: "India's optimism is rooted in substance, not sentiment. The country combines scientific talent, proven manufacturing excellence, a growing biologics pipeline and increasing policy support at a time when global supply chains are being rebalanced. We are seeing Indian companies move up the value chain, investing not only in capacity but also in technology, quality systems and innovation. The growth of the CDMO sector is a strong example of this evolution. While the journey is still unfolding, the trajectory is clear: India is positioning itself not just as a cost-efficient production base, but as a trusted global partner in biopharmaceutical development and manufacturing." 
The strategic significance is that Cytiva is positioning physical infrastructure around the entire journey from process development to manufacturing scale-up. That gives the company a role beyond equipment supply, placing it closer to the technical decisions customers make when they select, validate and scale bioprocessing platforms. 
Cytiva now has three major India facilities spanning manufacturing, experience-led training, Fast Trak process development and R&D, giving it one of the more integrated supplier footprints in the country. 
Sartorius and Repligen have also expanded their presence in India, adding to the growing life-sciences ecosystem around Hyderabad's Genome Valley. The cluster spans around 2,000 acres and is home to more than 200 life-science companies, including global players such as Novartis, GSK, Ferring Pharma and Lonza. Amgen has now announced plans to establish a new Science and Innovation Center in Genome Valley, further strengthening the cluster's global R&D profile. 
Merck Life Science took a related but distinct approach in February 2025, unveiling its Formulation & Technology Centre in Turbhe, Navi Mumbai, explicitly positioned as a hub serving not just India but the broader APAC, Middle East, and Africa region. Unlike the instrument-demonstration model used by Agilent and Thermo Fisher, Merck's centre is built around a specific technical bottleneck: helping pharmaceutical manufacturers navigate complex drug formulation, patent workarounds, and production scale-up, offering hands-on training, technical consulting, and troubleshooting support. The launch drew India's Biotechnology Industry Research Assistance Council (BIRAC) and the Indian Pharmaceutical Alliance (IPA) as institutional participants, a sign that these facilities are increasingly treated as national scientific infrastructure, not just vendor showrooms. Merck Life Science's India entity reported Rs 2,200 crore in revenue for the financial year ending March 2025, giving a sense of the scale of the India business these centres are meant to support. 
Thermo Fisher has continued layering on India investment beyond its Hyderabad launch. The company has also expanded its Bengaluru R&D Centre to advance antibody innovation, giving its India footprint a second dimension beyond customer-facing infrastructure: internal research capability. Together, its Hyderabad and Bengaluru investments illustrate a strategy that combines customer training, process development and proprietary R&D. 
Why Now: The Numbers Behind the Investment 
The timing is not coincidental. The suppliers are building infrastructure around a market that is becoming more complex, more biologics-heavy and more globally integrated. India's expanding CDMO base, growing biologics pipeline and policy push towards advanced biomanufacturing are increasing the number of companies that need access not just to equipment, but to application expertise, process-development support and trained personnel. 
India's single-use bioreactor market is projected to expand from $3.7 billion in 2025 to $10.9 billion by 2032, a 16.7 per cent CAGR, among the fastest-growing segments in global bioprocessing, and specifically flagged by industry analysts as the fastest-growing country market through 2030. That growth is playing out against a CDMO sector that JM Financial projects will roughly double from $7 billion in FY23 to $14 billion by 2028, a 14 per cent CAGR that outpaces the global CRDMO industry's roughly 9 per cent growth rate over the same period, directly increasing the number of India-based teams needing hands-on training on complex bioprocessing equipment. 
Estimates of the sector's overall size vary considerably depending on methodology and scope, with figures from other research firms ranging from roughly $8.5 billion to $25 billion for 2025 alone, but the doubling trajectory by 2028 is the consistent thread across most projections. India already holds a meaningful base to build from: the country produces an estimated 60 per cent of the world's vaccines and commands over 40 per cent of the US over-the-counter drug export market, giving global suppliers an existing manufacturing footprint to layer new biologics and cell-and-gene-therapy capacity onto rather than building from zero. 
The sentiment data backs this up. According to Cytiva's 2023 Global Biopharma Resilience Index, 65 per cent of biopharma executives in India expect biologics manufacturing in their country to increase dramatically over the next three years, 15 percentage points higher than the global average, while 46 per cent say they're actively focused on onshoring drug manufacturing or increasing domestic sourcing. More recent government figures suggest that this optimism is translating into a much larger industrial ecosystem. India's bioeconomy reached $195.3 billion in 2025, up from about $165 billion a year earlier, while the country now has more than 11,800 biotech startups. The government is targeting a $300 billion bioeconomy by 2030 under the BioE3 policy . These investments feed directly into India's stated national ambition to grow its bioeconomy to $300 billion by 2030 under the government's BioE3 policy, a target officials have repeatedly cited alongside Cytiva's Bengaluru and Pune expansions specifically. 
The Competitive Read 
The most revealing feature of this investment wave is not the number of facilities being announced, but what they are designed to do. Across Agilent, Thermo Fisher and Cytiva, the common model combines three functions: technology demonstration, applied technical training and customer support. That suggests the competitive battleground is shifting from the sale of equipment to the development of the ecosystem around that equipment. 
For suppliers, this creates a potentially more durable form of competitive advantage. A customer trained on a particular workflow, software environment and validation approach is not necessarily locked in—but switching suppliers can require retraining personnel, revalidating methods and adapting established processes. 
Taken together, these facilities suggest a new axis of competition among global biosuppliers in India, not just who sells the best mass spectrometer or bioreactor, but who builds the deepest local capability infrastructure around it. Agilent's four-site India network (Manesar, the Refurbishment Center, Hyderabad Biopharma Experience Center, and now Mumbai) mirrors Cytiva's three-site network (Pune, Bengaluru Fast Trak, Bengaluru R&D) and Thermo Fisher's India network similarly combines a Hyderabad CEC and BDC with an antibody-focused R&D capability in Bengaluru, three different global suppliers independently converging on the same "connected network of local hubs" model within roughly the same 12-month window. Merck Life Science's Navi Mumbai centre extends the pattern to formulation science specifically, and its explicit APAC/MEA regional framing suggests some of these India investments are being built to serve customers well beyond India's own borders. 
This also signals where each company is betting India's growth will concentrate. Agilent's Mumbai CEC leans toward pharma, diagnostics, food safety, and environmental testing, the more distributed, broad-based end of India's lab economy. 
"India's pharma and applied markets are evolving rapidly, with increasing focus on quality, compliance, and advanced analytical capabilities," said Bharat Bhardwaj, Vice President, Asia Pacific, Agilent Technologies , of the Mumbai center. "The CEC in Mumbai enhances how we support customers across India as they modernise laboratories, adopt new technologies, and meet both scientific and business objectives." 
Thermo Fisher and Cytiva's Hyderabad and Bengaluru/Pune investments lean specifically into biologics, cell and gene therapy, and bioprocessing, the higher-value, higher-growth segment tied directly to India's CDMO expansion and its $300 billion bioeconomy target. 
 The Strategic Logic Behind the Experience Centres 
That competitive read, however, needs to be separated from the suppliers' own positioning. Much of the language surrounding these facilities is understandably centred on training, capability-building and talent development. Those benefits may be genuine, but the same infrastructure can also strengthen a supplier's position within the customer's operating ecosystem. 
"Training," "capability-building," and "talent retention" are the words each company reaches for. But training a QC team exclusively on one supplier's proprietary workflows, or certifying staff on a specific analytical software suite inside a purpose-built center, has a second, less charitable effect: it raises the cost of ever switching to a competitor. Retraining staff, re-validating methods, and re-qualifying instruments under India's regulatory requirements are not small costs, and a lab that has invested in one supplier's ecosystem has real reasons to stay put even if a rival's hardware improves. 
In other words, capability-building and customer retention are not necessarily competing explanations. The same training programme can address a genuine industry skills gap while simultaneously deepening customer familiarity with a supplier's technology stack. 
One of the companies has said this almost explicitly. Its Experience Center was framed as addressing "the problem of retaining talent" by providing hands-on training that strengthens the skills of India's biotechnology workforce, rather than requiring engineers to travel abroad for training or relying on remote support. Another center is described as a facility to "learn, train, and collaborate" using bench-to-pilot scale equipment for process scale-up. In both cases, the public framing is training-first rather than sales-first. Yet the commercial effect can run in parallel: the more deeply customers are trained within a particular supplier's workflows, equipment and ecosystem, the more expensive and disruptive it can become to move elsewhere. 
Both readings fit the same set of facts, and it's worth noting that none of the source material for this report includes independent, third-party data on training completions or measurable skill outcomes from any of these centers. Every capability claim currently traces back to the supplier's own press materials, not an outside audit. 
The "India moment" framing deserves similar scrutiny. At least one of these Bioprocess Design Centers was announced explicitly as an expansion of an existing regional network that already included Singapore and Incheon, South Korea, meaning India was the newer addition to a build-out that started elsewhere in Asia, not the market driving the trend. That complicates the idea of a coordinated wave of investment uniquely timed to India's growth; it may be closer to India finally catching up to infrastructure its regional peers already had, which is a less flattering, if still commercially significant, version of the same story. 
A related pattern shows up in where these centers are actually located. Every facility named so far sits in one of India's five already-dominant life sciences metros, Mumbai, Navi Mumbai, Hyderabad, Bengaluru, and Pune. None of the companies surveyed here has announced a comparable center in tier-2 manufacturing clusters like Baddi in Himachal Pradesh or Ahmedabad and Vadodara in Gujarat, despite those regions carrying real existing production volume. If capability infrastructure keeps concentrating in the same handful of metro hubs, it risks reinforcing an already uneven distribution of scientific talent rather than closing the gap these companies say they're addressing. 
The challenge is particularly relevant for India's manufacturing expansion, because production capacity is not confined to the largest metros. If advanced training remains concentrated in the same five ecosystems, companies operating outside these clusters may continue to depend on travelling personnel, remote technical support or periodic access to supplier facilities. 
Outlook 
Expect the building spree itself to continue, even if the more skeptical reading above turns out to be closer to the truth than the suppliers' own framing. With India's CDMO sector on track to double by 2028 and its single-use bioreactor market growing at nearly 17 per cent annually, the commercial logic holds regardless of motive: the supplier that trains India's next generation of process engineers and QC scientists inside its own experience center gains a durable advantage that a superior spec sheet alone cannot replicate, precisely because switching costs are real once a team is trained. 
Whether that advantage is viewed primarily as capability-building, customer development or a form of ecosystem retention may ultimately matter less than the commercial reality: once suppliers become embedded in how India's scientists are trained, processes are developed and technologies are validated, their competitive position becomes considerably harder to dislodge. The next phase of this race, therefore, may not be about who builds the biggest experience centre, but who can turn these facilities into durable platforms for skills, application development, process innovation and, ultimately, global-scale manufacturing from India.

2026.10.01 13:17

Veolia Is Conducting Due Diligence to Acquire More Than 51%
Headquarters of SK ecoplant. 
SK ecoplant is handing over its stake in CENVIRO, a Malaysian waste management company, to the French environmental company Veolia. This move appears to be accelerating the company’s business restructuring centered on semiconductor and artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure, concluding the reorganization of its overseas eco-friendly businesses.
According to SK ecoplant on October 1, Veolia is conducting due diligence to acquire CENVIRO. The plan is to sign a share purchase agreement (SPA) to secure more than 51% by combining the entire stake held by SK ecoplant and a portion of the stake held by the Malaysian sovereign wealth fund Khazanah as early as this month. Currently, Khazanah holds a 70% stake in CENVIRO, and SK ecoplant holds a 30% stake.
The corporate value of CENVIRO is estimated to be between 800 billion won (about $615.38 million) and 900 billion won ($692.30 million). According to the business report, the book value of the 30% stake held by SK ecoplant was approximately 194.7 billion won ($149.76 million) as of the end of June, and through this sale, SK ecoplant is expected to secure funds of around 200 billion won ($153.84 million).
SK ecoplant acquired a 30% stake in CENVIRO for approximately 150 billion won ($115.38 million) in 2022. The initiative was to develop it into a hub for environmental business in Southeast Asia. However, as profitability fell short of expectations, the company has been pushing for a sale since April last year.
According to the business report on the Financial Supervisory Service’s Data Analysis, Retrieval and Transfer System, CENVIRO recorded sales of 165.1 billion won ($127.00 million) and a net income of 53.5 billion won ($41.15 million) in 2024. However, in 2025, despite sales increasing to 350.9 billion won ($269.92 million), it posted a net loss of 26.3 billion won ($20.23 million). For the first half of this year, sales stood at 181.3 billion won ($139.46 million), and net income was limited to approximately 26 million won ($20,000).
This sale is interpreted as a strategic move to lower the financial burden by unwinding capital tied up in low-profitability environmental businesses and to focus capital and capabilities on semiconductor and AI infrastructure. In fact, the company established an AI data center (DC) business division last month and is restructuring its organization and business around semiconductor and AI infrastructure.

Completion ceremony for JSR Micro Korea’s semiconductor materials plant in Ochang, Cheongju. (Photo: Chungcheongbuk-do Provincial Government) 
JSR Micro Korea, the South Korean subsidiary of Japan’s JSR Corp., completed a semiconductor materials plant on September 30 in the Ochang Foreign Investment Zone in Cheongju, North Chungcheong Province. The facility will produce metal oxide resist (MOR), a photoresist based on metal oxides for extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography.
​The facility is JSR’s first production base for EUV MOR. The company began commercializing MOR after acquiring US-based Inpria Corp. in 2021. The Ochang plant will carry out the final production process for MOR.
​MOR is an inorganic photoresist that offers higher etch resistance than organic-based materials. It can reduce pattern collapse during the lithography process, making it suitable for forming fine patterns. As EUV processes continue to scale down, MOR is attracting attention as a next-generation material that can complement conventional chemically amplified resists (CARs).
​Through the new production base, JSR aims to respond more quickly to demand from major domestic customers while strengthening its local production and quality-assurance capabilities. The facility is also expected to contribute to stabilizing the supply of key materials for South Korea’s semiconductor industry.
​JSR Micro Korea was established in Ochang in 2003 and has operated a business focused on display materials. The new plant establishes a domestic production system for next-generation semiconductor materials.
​Attendees at the completion ceremony included Tetsuro Hori, president and chief executive officer of JSR; Takahiro Iijima, president of JSR Micro Korea; Chungcheongbuk-do Gov. Shin Yong-han; and Shin Byeong-dae, vice mayor of Cheongju.

Communities In Schools of the Dallas Region Celebrates 15 Years of Golfing for a Greater Purpose
PressAdvantage
Dallas, Texas – September 24, 2026 – PRESSADVANTAGE – 
Communities In Schools of the Dallas Region (CIS Dallas) will celebrate 15 years of golfing for a greater purpose at its 15th Annual Kids Classic Golf Tournament , taking place Monday, December 7, 2026, at Cowboys Golf Club in Grapevine. Chaired by Karl Schmalz, the milestone tournament will feature a 9:30 a.m. shotgun start and, for the first time in the event’s history, bring supporters together at one of North Texas’ most distinctive golf destinations.
For 15 years, the Kids Classic Golf Tournament has helped CIS Dallas raise critical funds to support students throughout the Dallas region and across North Texas. Event participation helps provide the resources, encouragement and opportunities students need to overcome barriers, remain engaged in their education and build a path toward long-term success.
“This tournament has always been about much more than golf. It is about bringing people together around the belief that every student deserves the opportunity to succeed,” said Karl Schmalz, CIS Dallas Board Member and Kids Classic Golf Tournament Chair. “As we celebrate 15 years and move to Cowboys Golf Club, we are excited to offer an incredible experience while continuing to raise critical support for students across North Texas.”
Founded locally in 1985, Communities In Schools of the Dallas Region is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization dedicated to surrounding students with a community of support and empowering them to stay in school and achieve in life. CIS Dallas places trained professionals directly on school campuses, where they work alongside educators, administrators, families and community partners to provide coordinated, individualized support to K–12 students.
Through services focused on academics, attendance, behavior and mental health, social services, college and career readiness and basic needs, CIS Dallas addresses challenges that can interfere with a student’s ability to learn. These challenges may include housing instability, food or clothing insecurity, mental health needs, academic difficulties, inconsistent support systems and other circumstances that extend far beyond the classroom.
CIS Dallas currently serves students across 54 schools in 11 North Texas school districts. During the 2025–2026 school year, nearly 6,000 students received individualized case management services from CIS Dallas. Among students served, 99% were promoted to the next grade level, 96% of eligible high school seniors graduated and 100% remained in school.
“Every day, our team sees what students can accomplish when they have someone in their corner who understands their needs and connects them with the right support,” said Dr. Summer Rose, CEO of Communities In Schools of the Dallas Region. “The Kids Classic helps make that work possible. Every golfer, sponsor and partner is investing directly in students and helping ensure that challenges outside the classroom do not prevent them from reaching their full potential.”
This year’s 15th anniversary will offer a new experience for longtime supporters and first-time participants. Cowboys Golf Club recently underwent a multimillion-dollar renovation and features a redesigned course, a state-of-the-art driving range with Toptracer technology and the unique atmosphere of the world’s only NFL-themed golf club. The new setting gives CIS Dallas an opportunity to celebrate the tournament’s history while elevating the experience for the golfers, sponsors and community partners who make its impact possible.
CIS Dallas is also partnering with Mixed Media Creations (MMC) as the dedicated creative partner for this year’s tournament. The Dallas-Fort Worth full-service marketing and design studio will bring its expertise in branding, design, storytelling, and marketing to the event, helping elevate the tournament experience, strengthen sponsor visibility, and communicate the impact supporters are helping create for students. MMC works with businesses, nonprofits, and community organizations through a collaborative approach that combines creative strategy with purposeful design.
The mission of Communities In Schools of the Dallas Region (CIS) is to surround students with a community of support, empowering them to stay in school and achieve in life. CIS was founded in 1985 to improve the high school dropout rate in the Dallas area by providing academic, attendance, basic needs, and other support to students in local public schools. Today, in partnership with 11 school districts, CIS serves 54 Elementary, Middle, and High School campuses to serve 5,000 students who have been labeled “at-risk.”
Learn more, purchase tickets, see sponsorship opportunities, or make a donation at CISdallas.org .

DLA Troop Support, FDA interagency partnership informs DOW drug supply chain security policies
By Alison Welski 
DLA Troop Support Public Affairs 
Philadelphia  –  
Ensuring the security of the military pharmaceutical supply chain, Defense Logistics Agency Troop Support pharmacists came to a rare interagency data sharing agreement with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration. This agreement, meant to increase warfighter readiness, produced the latest dataset on 28 June.
A recommendation from the Inspector General prompted DLA and FDA to create a unique data-sharing agreement. This initiative was designed to address drug supply chain risks by developing new management rules and fostering partnerships amongst agencies.
“We co-chair the Pharmaceutical Supply Chain Risk Working Group alongside the Defense Health Agency,” said Air Force Lt. Col. Josh Stallings, CPOC chief, “to mitigate military drug supply chain risks, the group works in coordination with DLA and other federal partners to ensure consistent access to pharmaceuticals for the warfighter.”
This specific partnership with the FDA helps to further illuminate supply chain transparency issues surrounding these important pharmaceuticals by sharing industry information to better secure the military prescription drug supply chain.
“This data further informs our analysis of prescription drugs as the as they move through the supply chain,” said CPOC Pharmacist Navy Lt. Cmdr. Sean Szad.
However, this data gives the most precise information available to optimize warfighter readiness, said Szad.
“Our initial requests to the FDA mainly centered around countries of concern that could impact the availability of these drugs in some type of contingency.” Szad said.
Other data included in the agreement will help map the supply chain for DLA Troop Support’s monthly pharmaceutical orders and cross-reference them with the country of origin for each of drug, Szad continued.
“We are deeply interested in knowing where these drugs come from,” Stallings said, “because of their importance to the warfighter. In a contingency, we need to make sure to maintain reliable procurement.”
“We are huge fans of the FDA,” Stallings said. “They're a big fan of what we do, I think, because we develop these types of relationships. This interagency data sharing agreement is a big win for us here at Troop Support and for the warfighter we work for! I mean, it's a big win in huge way."

Heraeus Medical Components broke ground May 2 for a 17,000-square-foot addition to its facility in White Bear Township.
The company, one of the world's leading medical component manufacturers, currently employs 340 workers at 5030 Centerville Road, making it one of White Bear Township's largest employers. An additional 55 jobs will be created and a sum close to the two-digit-million-dollar-range will be invested in the expansion, qualifying Heraeus for nearly $500,000 under the Minnesota DEED Awards First Job Creation Funds Project.
Heraeus Medical Components General Manager Keith Foerster said: "We are excited to be launching our second expansion effort in the last four years. The proximity to our customers, availability of a talented workforce and our ongoing relationship with White Bear Township were key factors in our decision to expand in Minnesota."
Headquartered in Germany, Heraeus' precious metals and technology group is a global, private company founded 160 years ago. In the financial year 2012, Heraeus generated product revenues of almost $4 billion and previous metal trading revenues of $16 billion.
